approaches.title: Modular Lean proof of Cook's construction via a light-cone splicing lemma
approaches.method: Formalize Rule 110 as a map on configurations ℤ → Bool and prove Cook's emulation of cyclic tag systems (CTS) as a stack of independent layers. The load-bearing general lemma is locality (light-cone splicing): the restriction of step^[t] x to the interval [a+t, b−t] depends only on x restricted to [a, b]. With it, any finite pattern embedded in the periodic ether can be checked on a finite window by kernel computation (`decide` or `rfl` on List Bool, never `native_decide`), and the result transfers to the infinite configuration. Layers: (1) the ether is spacetime-periodic: it returns to a spatial shift of itself after its temporal period (Cook gives horizontal period 14 and vertical period 7); (2) each glider Cook uses (A through H and the variants in his construction) is a finite word that, spliced into ether, reappears translated after its period; (3) each collision in Cook's table, at each phase and offset the construction uses, produces the stated outgoing gliders, checked on a finite window; (4) a glider calculus: an abstract configuration (a list of glider type, phase and gap triples), an interpretation map into Rule 110 configurations, and a simulation theorem saying that for gaps above a stated threshold the CA evolution realizes the abstract collision rules; (5) Cook's encoding of CTS tape, appendants and the periodic right-hand program stream, with a theorem that one CTS step corresponds to a bounded number of abstract collision rounds.
steps: Define `rule110`, `step`, shift, and prove the light-cone splicing lemma by induction on t.
Encode the ether word and prove its spacetime periodicity on a finite window; lift to ℤ with the splicing lemma.
Transcribe Cook's glider catalogue and collision table from the open-access Complex Systems paper into Lean data; prove each entry by bounded kernel computation.
Define the abstract glider-list semantics and prove the simulation theorem for well-separated configurations.
Define cyclic tag systems in Lean and Cook's encoding; prove the one-step correspondence and the main theorem by induction on CTS steps.
Check `#print axioms` lists only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound; write a report in the format of the Thompson Lean reports.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean 4 module whose main theorem states: for every cyclic tag system and input word there is an initial Rule 110 configuration (ether plus a finite perturbation on the left and a periodic glider stream on the right) and a decoding map such that the CA evolution encodes every CTS step. It must compile with no sorry and only the three standard axioms, with every glider and collision fact a proved lemma.
approaches.failure_signature: A collision required by the encoding that the kernel check refutes at the phase or gap the construction needs (a gap in Cook's table, itself a publishable finding), or kernel computations on the required windows that are too large to complete without native_decide, forcing the project to stall at layer 3.

references.note: Cook 2004, Universality in elementary cellular automata
Neary and Woods 2006, P-completeness of cellular automaton Rule 110
Mathlib 4; Mathlib.Computability provides Turing machine and partial-recursive definitions to which CTS universality can later be connected

approaches.missing: Proof-engineering volume rather than new mathematics: Cook's construction has many glider spacings and timing constraints, and kernel-only evaluation of large windows may be slow. A month is likely enough for layers 1 to 3, not the full chain.

approaches.title: Independent exhaustive audit of Cook's glider and collision table
approaches.method: Before or alongside formalization, re-derive from scratch every fact Cook's construction depends on, using code written without reference to Cook's tables except for the final comparison. Enumerate all gliders on the ether background up to period 200 and width 100 using de Bruijn-diagram search for spacetime-periodic patterns. For every ordered pair of gliders used by the construction, simulate the collision at every relative phase and every integer gap in the range the construction allows, and record the outgoing glider multiset with phases. Then run the full construction for small cyclic tag systems (including Cook's worked example and randomly generated CTS with up to 6 appendants of length up to 6) for at least 10^7 generations with bit-parallel simulation, and decode the CTS tape from the glider stream at each emulated step, comparing with a direct CTS interpreter.
steps: Implement a bit-sliced Rule 110 simulator and a de Bruijn-diagram glider finder; verify against the published list of Rule 110 gliders.
Produce a machine-readable collision table (JSON) over all phases and gaps used by the construction, with SHA-256 of the generating code and output.
Diff the table against a transcription of Cook's table; classify every discrepancy as transcription error, phase-convention difference or genuine mismatch.
Run end-to-end emulations of at least 100 random CTS and compare decoded tapes step by step with a reference interpreter.
approaches.decisive_result: Either a complete match (every collision the construction needs behaves as stated at every allowed gap, and all end-to-end emulations decode correctly for 10^7 generations), which hands layer 3 of a formal proof a verified target, or a specific (glider pair, phase, gap) triple whose outcome differs from Cook's table and breaks an emulation.
approaches.failure_signature: The audit cannot settle universality either way by itself; it fails as an approach if the gap ranges the construction needs cannot be extracted unambiguously from the paper, so the audit checks a reconstruction rather than Cook's proof.

references.note: Cook 2004, source of the glider catalogue and collision table to audit
Neary and Woods 2006, gives an alternative account of the construction's timing

approaches.title: Verified certificate checker: reduce the proof to a finite spacetime tile set
approaches.method: Instead of proving Cook's construction lemma by lemma, prove once in Lean that a small checker is sound, and let external search produce the certificate. The spacetime diagram of Cook's construction for an arbitrary CTS is assembled from finitely many rectangular spacetime tiles (ether blocks, glider segments, collision blocks), and the program side is periodic while the data side varies only through which tiles are chosen. Define in Lean a certificate as a finite tile set with edge labels (boundary words) plus a context-free or regular grammar describing admissible tile arrangements for any CTS. The checker verifies (a) each tile is a valid Rule 110 spacetime patch, by kernel computation, (b) adjacent tiles agree on shared boundary words, (c) the grammar generates, for each CTS step, an arrangement whose decoded output equals the CTS successor. Soundness theorem: if the checker accepts, the universality statement holds. This fails differently from approach 1: the human-proof burden shrinks to the soundness lemma and the grammar semantics, while the computational burden moves to certificate generation outside Lean.
steps: Specify tiles, boundary words and the arrangement grammar in Lean; prove the soundness theorem using the light-cone splicing lemma.
Write an external generator that runs the construction on many CTS, cuts the spacetime diagram into tiles, deduplicates them and infers the arrangement grammar.
Run the checker inside Lean by kernel reduction on the certificate; iterate on tile size if kernel cost is prohibitive.
Prove the grammar-to-CTS correspondence by induction on CTS steps.
approaches.decisive_result: Lean accepts the certificate, and the soundness theorem plus the checker run yields the universality theorem with only standard axioms. A secondary artifact is the tile count, a compact measure of the construction's complexity.
approaches.failure_signature: The tile decomposition does not close: arrangements depend on unbounded gap values in a way no regular or context-free grammar captures, or the tile set needed exceeds what kernel reduction can check in reasonable time.

references.note: Cook 2004, the construction to be tiled
Coq proof of BB(5), a precedent for verified deciders checking large externally generated case analyses in a proof assistant

approaches.missing: No existing tile-level description of Cook's construction; the grammar-inference step is research.

approaches.title: Decidability route: regular invariants for the (2,3) machine on periodic backgrounds
approaches.method: Fix the decision problem first, since the (2,3) machine has no halt state: say 'does the head ever reach cell n' or 'does the tape ever contain word v within distance n of the origin', which is how Smith's emulation reads off computation. Restrict to eventually periodic tapes u^ω · w · v^ω. Use the bbchallenge decider family, adapted to non-halting machines: closed tape languages, finite-automata reduction (FAR) and translated-cycler detection. They search for a regular language L of configurations that contains the initial configuration, is closed under the step relation, and implies the property or its negation. Enumerate background pairs (u, v) with |u|, |v| ≤ 8 and windows |w| ≤ 12. If a uniform regular invariant family appears (for example, the machine reduces on every periodic background to a counter or pushdown system whose reachability is decidable), state and prove it in Lean as a decidability theorem. Systematic non-existence of small invariants, together with growth patterns resembling Smith's system 0, is evidence in the other direction and identifies the hardest background classes.
steps: Write the (2,3) rule table and a reference simulator; fix the observable (head-position or word-occurrence predicate) as the decision problem.
Port FAR and closed-tape-language deciders to non-halting predicates; validate on machines whose behaviour is known.
Run the enumeration over (u, w, v) and record which configurations admit regular invariants and with how many states.
If invariants follow a pattern, generalize by hand and formalize the decidability proof in Lean 4; otherwise publish the census of undecided cases.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean-checked theorem that the chosen predicate is decidable for all eventually periodic initial tapes, which refutes universality under that definition. Short of that, a census giving, for each background up to the bound, either a verified regular invariant or an explicit undecided configuration.
approaches.failure_signature: Many small backgrounds, including the blank one, resist all regular invariants up to large state counts, while showing irregular, nested head motion; the decidability route then probably cannot succeed.

references.note: Smith 2020, Universality of Wolfram's 2,3 Turing machine (non-periodic background)
Woods and Neary 2009, survey defining standard, semi-weak and weak universality
Busy Beaver Challenge: decider methods (FAR, closed tape languages) for proving non-halting via regular invariants

approaches.missing: Mathematics beyond current automation if the machine is in fact universal on periodic backgrounds; adapting halting-oriented deciders to observables is new work.

approaches.title: Construction route: replace Smith's non-periodic tape with a periodic refuel gadget
approaches.method: Smith's proof is a chain: the (2,3) machine emulates system 0, which emulates a sequence of intermediate systems ending in a cyclic tag system, and the infinite non-periodic tape supplies the structures the chain consumes. Implement each layer as an executable specification and instrument the emulation to find exactly which layer consumes non-periodic structure, and what that structure is (for example, blocks whose lengths grow with the number of emulated steps). Then search for a replacement: a finite gadget on a periodic background that regenerates the consumed structure on demand. Neary and Woods' weakly universal small machines show this kind of periodic-background refuelling can work. The search runs over short periodic background words and finite gadgets (SAT or bounded model checking on the layer's step relation), with the requirement that the composed system still emulates the CTS.
steps: Implement Smith's systems 0 through 5 and the CTS layer as executable specs, with cross-checking simulation from a common CTS input.
Instrument the emulation to log the background symbols consumed per emulated CTS step and fit their growth law.
Formulate a SAT or bounded-model-checking search for a periodic background plus finite gadget that produces the consumed structure; run for background periods up to 40.
If a candidate is found, verify by long simulation and then formalize the composed emulation in Lean.
approaches.decisive_result: An explicit eventually periodic initial tape for which the (2,3) machine emulates a universal CTS, verified by simulation for at least 10^6 emulated steps and then proved in Lean. Even without success, the instrumented chain is a precise statement of what the non-periodic tape contributes, which the current literature lacks.
approaches.failure_signature: The consumed structure grows superlinearly in a way no finite gadget on a periodic background can produce (for example, its growth law implies the background must encode an unbounded counter), or the search exhausts all gadgets up to the size bound.

references.note: Smith 2020, the emulation chain to instrument
Neary and Woods 2009, Small weakly universal Turing machines (periodic-background constructions)
Wolfram 2,3 Turing Machine Research Prize page with the proof materials

approaches.missing: Possibly a genuinely new idea; the search space for gadgets may be far too large.

approaches.title: Formalize Smith's proof and bound the computational power of its initial tape
approaches.method: Machine-check what is currently claimed, with the definitional issue stated exactly. Formalize in Lean 4 Smith's theorem: for every CTS there is a computable initial tape on which the (2,3) machine emulates it. Then prove a theorem about the tape's complexity, which is what the dispute is about. Candidate statements: the tape is generated by a fixed finite-state transducer from the CTS description and a fixed infinite word; it is a fixed morphic or automatic sequence modified by a finite prefix; or it is computable in linear time by a non-universal device. Each turns 'the encoding smuggles in computation' into a checkable claim. If the tape is automatic or morphic, the result places the (2,3) machine in a precisely named universality class between weak universality (periodic background) and Smith's notion.
steps: Formalize the (2,3) machine, CTS and Smith's intermediate systems in Lean; prove each emulation step.
Extract the explicit initial-tape generator from the proof and formalize it as a function.

Prove the generator lies in a named weak class (finite transducer over a fixed sequence, automatic sequence, or linear-time and non-universal), or show it cannot, by exhibiting an encoding step that requires unbounded computation.
Write a short mapping of the critics' objections onto the formal statements.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module proving Smith's theorem together with a proved upper bound on the complexity of the required tape (for example 'the tape is k-automatic'). That settles the definitional dispute in the form 'universal under definition D', even though it leaves the periodic-background case open.
approaches.failure_signature: Formalization uncovers a gap in Smith's chain that cannot be closed, or the tape generator turns out to need unbounded computation in a way that makes every weak-class statement false.

references.note: Smith 2020, the proof to formalize
Woods and Neary 2009, universality notions
Mathlib.Computability: Turing machine models, partial recursive functions

approaches.missing: Smith's chain is long (about 40 pages of construction); the full formalization is likely beyond a month, though the tape-complexity analysis can be done on the informal proof first.

approaches.title: Automated synthesis of a cyclic-tag emulation from the complete collision graph
approaches.method: Treat universality search as program synthesis over glider collisions. First compute the complete set of Rule 54 gliders on the standard ether up to period 120 and width 80 (de Bruijn diagrams), and the full binary collision table over all phases and gaps (outgoing gliders, phase shifts, and whether the outcome depends on the gap). Then search the collision graph for the four functional components of a Cook-style CTS emulation: stationary or slow 'tape' gliders encoding 0 and 1; a periodic left-moving 'program' stream encoding appendants; an annihilation or conversion reaction that reads the leading tape symbol; and a reaction that appends or deletes appendant material conditionally. Encode timing and spacing constraints as an SMT problem (z3, integer gaps modulo the ether period) and search for satisfying assignments that emulate a 2-appendant CTS. A solution is validated by direct simulation and then formalized as in the Rule 110 approach.
steps: Compute and publish the glider catalogue with periods, velocities and phases; compare with Martínez, Adamatzky and McIntosh 2006.
Compute the complete binary collision table and identify collisions that are gap-sensitive, the raw material for conditional behaviour.
Encode CTS-emulation components as SMT constraints over glider choices and gaps; search with increasing component sizes.
Validate any candidate by simulating a small universal CTS for 10^7 generations and decoding.
approaches.decisive_result: An explicit initial configuration (ether, finite seed, periodic stream) on which Rule 54 emulates arbitrary CTS, validated by simulation and then proved in Lean. Short of that, a proof that the collision graph restricted to gliders up to the bound lacks a conditional-append reaction, which pins down what a universal construction would need.
approaches.failure_signature: The SMT search finds no conditional reaction among gliders up to the bound; every collision outcome is independent of the data it would need to read. That is evidence that the bound is too small or that the second (impossibility) approach is the right one.

references.note: Martínez, Adamatzky and McIntosh 2006, Phenomenology of glider collisions in cellular automaton Rule 54 and associated logical gates (Chaos, Solitons & Fractals 28:100). The DOI listed in problems.json resolves to a different paper.
Cook 2004, template for the CTS-emulation architecture
Z3 SMT solver for the timing-constraint search

approaches.missing: Conditional (data-reading) reactions may not exist among small gliders; the search may need structures no one has catalogued.

approaches.title: Impossibility route: a potential function on glider dynamics forcing ballistic decay
approaches.method: Try to prove that Rule 54 cannot be universal in a precise sense, for example that on every finite perturbation of the ether the long-run behaviour is decidable. Strategy: (a) prove a decomposition theorem that every configuration differing from the ether on a finite set evolves, after a transient bounded in terms of the perturbation's width, into a superposition of catalogued gliders separated by ether, using a de Bruijn-diagram argument that any non-ether, non-glider region shrinks; (b) compute the full collision algebra and look for a potential Φ (a weighted glider count, or a count weighted by velocity class) that never increases in any collision and strictly decreases in some. If Φ exists and the number of gliders produced by a collision is bounded, every finite perturbation reaches, in finitely many collisions, a state of non-interacting outgoing gliders. Then 'eventual configuration' is computable, which rules out universality for the standard definition with finite seeds. The integrable reversible RCA54 of Bobenko et al., a different automaton whose name and local rule are related, has solitons that only phase-shift on collision; checking whether ECA 54's ether-restricted dynamics inherit such a conservation law is a concrete sub-question.
steps: Compute the collision algebra (outcome multiset for each glider pair, phase and gap) from the approach-1 catalogue.
Solve an integer linear program for weights making Φ non-increasing over all catalogued collisions; record strict decreases.
Attempt the decomposition theorem: prove by exhaustive de Bruijn analysis that non-glider defects shrink, giving a bound on transient length.
If both hold, formalize: decomposition plus potential implies decidability of the eventual glider content; state precisely what this excludes (universality with finite seeds on ether).
approaches.decisive_result: A proof, ideally Lean-checked, that for every finite perturbation of the ether the multiset of eventual outgoing gliders is computable. This rules out universality from finite seeds on ether, and the result states exactly which universality notions remain open (for example, infinite periodic program streams).
approaches.failure_signature: The ILP is infeasible, meaning some collision cycle increases every candidate potential (glider multiplication), or an exhaustive search finds a finite perturbation that produces unboundedly many gliders (a 'gun' or breeder). Both suggest universality is plausible and point back to approach 1.

references.note: Martínez, Adamatzky and McIntosh 2006, Rule 54 glider collisions
Bobenko, Bordemann, Gunn and Pinkall 1993, On two integrable cellular automata (the reversible RCA54, a related but distinct system)

approaches.missing: Infinite periodic program streams (as in Cook's Rule 110 proof) escape a finite-seed impossibility argument, so even success settles only one universality notion.

approaches.title: Lean-certified completeness of the Rule 54 glider catalogue up to explicit bounds
approaches.method: Both other approaches depend on knowing all gliders, and current catalogues are lists of what has been seen, not completeness theorems. Prove in Lean 4: every pattern that is spacetime-periodic on the ether, with period p ≤ P and width w ≤ W, is one of the listed gliders up to phase and translation. The method is de Bruijn-diagram enumeration. Periodic patterns of period p correspond to cycles in a finite graph whose vertices are width-2p words, so completeness reduces to enumerating cycles in finite graphs. Extract the enumeration as a certificate (cycle list plus a proof that no other cycle passes the ether boundary conditions) and check it in Lean by kernel reduction. Pick P and W so the kernel check stays feasible (P = 24 first, then extend).
steps: Define the de Bruijn graph for period-p spacetime patterns in Lean and prove the correspondence theorem (periodic pattern ⇔ graph cycle).
Generate the cycle enumeration externally for each p ≤ P with ether boundary conditions.
Check the certificate in Lean; derive the completeness theorem for the glider list.
Repeat for the binary collision table: prove that outcomes for all pairs from the complete list are as tabulated.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean theorem 'the gliders of Rule 54 on ether with period ≤ P and width ≤ W are exactly G_1 … G_k' plus a verified collision table. This does not settle universality, but turns the search space of approaches 1 and 2 from an observation into a proved object.
approaches.failure_signature: The de Bruijn graphs for useful P are too large for kernel checking (they grow as 2^(2p) vertices), capping the theorem at a P too small to include the gliders Martínez et al. used for gates.

references.note: Martínez, Adamatzky and McIntosh 2006, catalogue to be certified

approaches.title: Lean: left-permutivity, Jen's two-column theorem and conditional extensions
approaches.method: Formalize the only rigorous progress on Prize problem 1 and push it as far as it goes. Rule 30 is x_i^{t+1} = x_{i−1}^t XOR (x_i^t OR x_{i+1}^t). It is left-permutive: x_{i−1}^t = x_i^{t+1} XOR (x_i^t OR x_{i+1}^t), so two adjacent columns determine everything to their left. Jen (1990, announced 1986) proved that no two columns of the single-seed pattern can both be eventually periodic. Prove in Lean: (a) the reconstruction lemma; (b) if columns i and i+1 are eventually periodic with period p, every column to the left is eventually periodic with period p; (c) Jen's theorem, from the fact that the left boundary of the light cone moves left one cell per step, contradicting periodicity of the reconstructed region. Then attempt new conditional theorems with explicit hypotheses, for example: if the center column is eventually periodic with period p from time t₀, then column +1 is not eventually periodic and its subword complexity grows at least linearly; or, the periodic-diagonal region on the left (Wolfram's observation) cannot reach the center column before time f(p).
steps: Define Rule 30 and the single-seed evolution on ℤ × ℕ; prove the light-cone and left-permutivity lemmas.
Prove the reconstruction and periodicity-propagation lemmas; derive Jen's two-column theorem.
Formulate and attempt the conditional single-column statements; record which hypotheses each needs.
Report as in the Thompson Lean reports, with axioms checked.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module proving Jen's theorem (no two columns both eventually periodic) with only standard axioms, plus at least one new conditional theorem about the center column whose hypothesis is stated explicitly. A proof of non-periodicity itself would settle Prize problem 1.
approaches.failure_signature: All conditional extensions reduce back to assuming information about a second column; the left-permutivity method then provably cannot reach a single column without new input.

references.note: Jen 1990, Aperiodicity in one-dimensional cellular automata, Physica D 45:3
Wolfram 2019, prize announcement; summarizes Jen's result and the left-permutivity reconstruction
Rule 30 Prize problems

approaches.missing: Jen's theorem is tractable; a genuinely new single-column result needs a mathematical idea no one has yet found.

approaches.title: Extend the column to 10^10–10^11 bits with a pre-registered density and period test
approaches.method: Extend the known prefix beyond the published billion bits and pre-register what the extension can and cannot show. Computing n center bits needs about n²/2 cell updates, but the light cone can be trimmed: cells at distance d from the center at time t only matter if d ≤ n − t. With bit-sliced 64-wide words on GPUs this gives roughly 10^19 to 10^20 word operations for n = 10^10, which is feasible on a modest cluster. Pre-register: (a) exclusion of every eventual period p ≤ n/3 with transient ≤ n/3, using a suffix-array or Z-function scan; (b) a density test, the running deviation D(n) = #1s − n/2 compared with the law-of-iterated-logarithm envelope √(2n log log n)/2 expected for an i.i.d. fair sequence, with pass and fail bands fixed in advance; (c) block-frequency and linear-complexity profiles (Berlekamp–Massey) at block lengths 1 to 20. The result is computational evidence, recorded as data_kind 'computational', not a proof.
steps: Validate the simulator against the published billion-bit dataset (SHA-256 match).
Write result.json with hypotheses, bands and planned outputs before running beyond 10^9.
Run to n = 10^10 (stretch 10^11) with checkpointing; publish the prefix checksum and a fetch script, not the data.
Run the period-exclusion scan, the LIL density test and Berlekamp–Massey linear complexity; record verdicts.
approaches.decisive_result: A certified statement that no eventual period with transient and period each ≤ n/3 exists in the first n = 10^10 bits, and density deviations inside or outside the pre-registered LIL band. A detected period would refute problem 1 outright.
approaches.failure_signature: Compute or memory limits stop the run below 10^10, so it adds little beyond the published billion bits; or the trimming is shown to be wrong because the result disagrees with the reference prefix.

approaches.title: Restricted-model lower bounds: the column is not generated by small automata
approaches.method: Attack weak forms of problems 1 and 3 that are provable. Problem 3 asks for a lower bound on the effort to compute bit n, and unrestricted lower bounds are out of reach, but lower bounds against restricted models are finite questions. (a) For each base k in {2, 3, 4} and state count s ≤ 12, prove that no deterministic finite automaton with output (DFAO) reading n in base k reproduces the first N center bits. Encode as SAT (variables for transition and output tables; constraints from each prefix bit) and extract unsatisfiability certificates, which are DRAT proofs checkable by a verified checker. (b) Use Walnut to test whether the prefix is consistent with low-complexity morphic generation. (c) Prove in Lean, from (a) and the definitions, the theorem 'the center column is not k-automatic with ≤ s states'. That theorem implies, for example, that no constant-memory streaming algorithm over base-k digits of n computes the column with that much memory.
steps: Generate SAT instances for (k, s) pairs over a prefix of N = 10^6 bits (smaller if unsatisfiability is reached earlier).
Solve with a DRAT-producing solver; check proofs with a verified checker.
Formalize the DFAO definition in Lean and state the non-automaticity theorems; import the certificate check by kernel-verified decoding of the minimal refuting prefix.
Record the largest (k, s) reached and the shortest refuting prefix for each.
approaches.decisive_result: Lean-checked theorems 'the Rule 30 center column is not generated by any base-k DFAO with at most s states' for stated (k, s). These are new and weak; their value is a precise, citable lower bound in a restricted model, and any satisfiable instance that extends to 10^9 bits would be a striking structural discovery.
approaches.failure_signature: SAT instances become intractable at small s (for example s ≤ 6), giving results too weak to matter; or proofs need native_decide-level computation that Lean cannot do in kernel.

approaches.title: Sign-pattern theorem via additive D-stability and sign stability
approaches.method: Reformulate. With linearization J at a stable steady state and diagonal diffusion D ≥ 0, a Turing instability is J stable with J − k²D unstable for some k > 0. Absorbing k² into D, the pattern P is Turing-capable (all species may diffuse) iff some realization J of P is stable but not additively D-stable, that is, J − D is unstable for some nonnegative diagonal D (Cross 1978). Lemma A: sign-stable patterns, characterized combinatorially by Quirk–Ruppert and Jeffries–Klee–van den Driessche (nonpositive diagonal, no positive 2-cycles, no cycles of length ≥ 3, nonzero determinant, a colour test), stay sign-stable when negative diagonal is added, hence are Turing-incapable. Conjecture B for n = 3: P is Turing-capable iff P is potentially stable and not sign-stable. Prove B by case analysis over which Jeffries condition fails (a 3-cycle, a positive self-loop, a mutualistic 2-cycle, or the colour test). For each case give an explicit parametric family (J(ε), D) that is stable, satisfying the 3×3 Routh–Hurwitz conditions a₁ > 0, a₃ > 0, a₁a₂ > a₃, with det(J − D) of the wrong sign or Routh–Hurwitz violated for J − D. For m < n diffusing species, D is supported on the diffusing set S, and the analogous criterion involves principal submatrices of J off S (Satnoianu et al. 2000).
steps: Prove in Lean: for 3×3 real matrices, define stability by the Routh–Hurwitz inequalities on the characteristic polynomial coefficients, and prove that the Turing condition is equivalent to 'not additively D-stable'.
Prove Lemma A (sign-stable implies Turing-incapable) from the Jeffries conditions.
For each failure mode of sign stability, construct witness families and prove the inequalities with nlinarith or polyrith.
Extend to restricted diffusion sets S ⊂ {1,2,3} and state the theorem for each m.
Check the theorem against approach 2's enumeration (any disagreement is a counterexample to B).
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean-checked theorem: for n = 3 and each diffusing set S, the Turing-capable sign patterns are exactly those satisfying an explicit combinatorial condition (conjecturally 'potentially stable and not S-restricted sign-stable'), with zero disagreements against the exhaustive enumeration.
approaches.failure_signature: The enumeration finds a potentially stable, non-sign-stable pattern that is Turing-incapable (every stable realization is additively D-stable without being sign-stable), so Conjecture B is false and the characterization needs a finer invariant.

references.note: Turing 1952, The chemical basis of morphogenesis
Cross 1978, Three types of matrix stability (D-stability, additive D-stability)
Jeffries, Klee and van den Driessche 1977, When is a matrix sign stable?
Quirk and Ruppert 1965, Qualitative economics and the stability of equilibrium
Satnoianu, Menzinger and Maini 2000, Turing instabilities in general systems

approaches.missing: Mathlib lacks a ready Routh–Hurwitz theorem connecting coefficient inequalities to root location; for n = 3 it must be proved, or stability defined by the coefficient conditions with that equivalence proved separately.

approaches.title: Exact exhaustive enumeration for n = 3 and n = 4 with certificates
approaches.method: Decide Turing-capability for every sign pattern exactly, not by sampling. For n = 3 there are 3^9 = 19,683 patterns, about 3,400 up to relabelling. For each pattern and diffusing set S, the question ∃J consistent with P, ∃D ≥ 0 supported on S, ∃k: J stable and J − k²D unstable is a sentence in the existential theory of the reals, decidable by cylindrical algebraic decomposition or nlsat. Pipeline: (1) random-search for a numerical witness (log-uniform entries, D spanning six orders of magnitude); (2) if found, rationalize and verify exactly (rational arithmetic, Routh–Hurwitz), and emit the witness as a Lean `norm_num` lemma; (3) otherwise run Redlog CAD or z3 nlsat on the exact sentence and keep the 'unsat' result, or prove incapability from sign stability (approach 1, Lemma A). For n = 4, 3^16 ≈ 4.3 × 10^7 patterns, about 1.8 × 10^6 up to relabelling. Numerical witnesses should settle most capable patterns; the unresolved remainder goes to nlsat with a time cap, and capped cases are reported as open. Compare with the Marcon et al. 2016 and Scholes et al. 2019 atlases pattern by pattern.
steps: Canonicalize patterns under node relabelling (respecting S) and generate the work list.
Run witness search with exact rational verification; export capable witnesses as Lean lemmas.
Run CAD or nlsat on unresolved patterns; record certificates or timeouts.
Cross-check with the published atlases; publish the classification table with SHA-256 and reproduction scripts.
approaches.decisive_result: A complete n = 3 table (every pattern × S labelled capable with an exact rational witness, or incapable with a CAD/nlsat certificate or sign-stability proof), and an n = 4 table with the fraction left undecided stated. Any capable pattern that a published atlas lists as non-Turing, or the reverse, is reported.
approaches.failure_signature: CAD or nlsat times out on a substantial set of n = 3 patterns, so incapability cannot be certified and the table is incomplete even at n = 3.

approaches.title: Genericity for n ≥ 3 via counting non-sign-stable patterns and a 3-node embedding lemma
approaches.method: Prove the genericity conjecture without first characterizing every n. Embedding lemma: if a principal subpattern on 3 nodes is Turing-capable (with a stable realization), and the remaining nodes have negative self-loops, then the full pattern is Turing-capable. Proof sketch: realize the 3-node block with a witness, give other nodes strong self-damping −M, and scale off-block couplings by ε. For small ε and large M, the eigenvalues of J and of J − k²D are perturbations of the block eigenvalues plus values near −M, so stability and the instability persist by continuity of eigenvalues (Gershgorin plus a Rouché-type argument). Counting lemma: among n-node patterns with all diagonal entries negative, the fraction with no 3-node principal subpattern from the n = 3 capable list tends to 0 as n → ∞. This holds because the n = 3 list is nonempty and the C(n,3) triples are only weakly dependent, so a second-moment (Janson) bound applies. Together these give: almost all n-node patterns with negative self-loops are Turing-capable. Weaker hypotheses on the diagonal (for example, at least one self-loop) need a refined embedding.
steps: State and prove the embedding lemma (eigenvalue continuity under block-diagonal dominance) in Lean, or rigorously on paper if Mathlib's spectral continuity is insufficient.
Take the n = 3 capable list from approach 2 and prove the counting lemma via Janson's inequality.
Combine into the genericity theorem; state precisely the class of patterns (diagonal sign assumptions) it covers.
Check numerically against approach 2's n = 4 table: predicted capable fraction versus measured.
approaches.decisive_result: A theorem: the fraction of n-node sign patterns (in the stated class) that are Turing-capable tends to 1 as n → ∞, with an explicit rate, checked against the n = 4 enumeration.
approaches.failure_signature: The embedding lemma fails because coupling to the other nodes destroys stability or instability in ways small ε cannot control for some sign configurations, or the n = 4 enumeration shows a capable fraction inconsistent with the bound.

approaches.title: Lean: Price equation and the regression Hamilton's rule as an exact finite identity
approaches.method: Formalize the finite-population statements both sides of the 2010–2011 dispute rely on. Population: a Finset of individuals with breeding value g_i, social partners' breeding value g'_i and fitness w_i (real, mean w̄ > 0). Theorem 1 (Price, no transmission bias): w̄ Δḡ = Cov(w, g). Theorem 2 (least-squares decomposition): with c := −β_{wg·g'} and b := β_{wg'·g} the partial regression coefficients from the 2×2 normal equations (assuming the regressors' covariance matrix is nonsingular), Cov(w, g) = Var(g)(r b − c) with r := Cov(g', g)/Var(g). Corollary (regression HR): if Var(g) > 0, then Δḡ > 0 ⇔ r b > c. Theorem 3 (content condition): if fitness is exactly additive, w_i = α − c₀ g_i + b₀ g'_i, then the regression b, c equal b₀, c₀ in every population state, so the rule predicts change from parameters fixed in advance. Theorem 4: if fitness has an interaction term d g_i g'_i, the regression b and c depend on the population state, so b and c measured in one generation do not predict the next. These separate reading (ii), an identity, from reading (i), a theorem with content.
steps: Define finite-population mean, covariance and partial regression coefficients over Finset sums in Lean.
Prove Theorems 1 and 2 and the corollary with field_simp, ring and positivity.
Prove Theorem 3 (parameter recovery under additivity) and Theorem 4 (state dependence under synergy), giving explicit rational states for the latter.
Write the mapping document: each disputed sentence from Nowak et al. 2010, Gardner et al. 2011 and Birch and Okasha 2015 assigned to Theorems 1–4 or to approach 2's counterexamples.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module with Theorems 1–4 compiled with only standard axioms, and a mapping table assigning each disputed claim to a formal statement. This settles which claims are identities and which have content under which hypotheses.
approaches.failure_signature: None expected for Theorems 1–3, which are classical. The approach fails as a resolution if the mapping shows the disputants mean incompatible definitions of 'Hamilton's rule' that no single formal statement captures; the mapping would then document the equivocation instead.

approaches.title: Formal counterexamples: synergistic games where parameter-based rb > c mispredicts
approaches.method: Settle reading (iii), when the rule is false, by explicit, Lean-checked counterexamples in standard population-genetic models. Model: a two-player game with payoffs to a focal individual: cooperate against cooperate R = b − c + d, cooperate against defect −c, defect against cooperate b, defect against defect 0. Here d is the synergy term, and assortment is given by relatedness r through the probability that partners share type. Under weak selection, with linear fitness and the probability of a cooperator partner given focal type p_C = r + (1 − r)p, the expected change in cooperator frequency has sign (r b − c) + d·φ(r, p), with φ an explicit polynomial. Choose rational (b, c, d, r, p) with r b > c but Δp < 0, and the reverse, and prove both in Lean by norm_num. Also prove the general form, the generalized Hamilton's rule with the synergy correction (Queller's form), as a theorem, so the counterexample marks where the simple rule's scope ends. Second family: a frequency-dependent threshold game where the sign of Δp flips with p at fixed (b, c, r), showing that no fixed parameter pair predicts the direction everywhere.
steps: Define the game, assortment and expected allele-frequency change in Lean.
Derive the closed form for Δp and prove the synergy-corrected rule.
Prove two explicit counterexample instances and the frequency-flip instance with norm_num.
Add these as the (iii) entries of the approach-1 mapping table.
approaches.decisive_result: Lean theorems exhibiting model states in which the parameter-based rule r b > c and the actual direction of selection disagree, alongside a theorem stating the corrected rule. This is the formal refutation the problem's falsifier asks about for the parameter reading, while approach 1 shows the regression reading is never refuted.
approaches.failure_signature: None for the mathematics. The approach fails as a contribution if reviewers judge the model class non-standard; mitigate by using the exact models of van Veelen et al. 2017 and Lehmann and Keller 2006.

approaches.title: Computational phase map of when parameter-based Hamilton's rule predicts selection
approaches.method: Map the boundary between readings (i) and (iii) across model space, not just at isolated counterexamples. Model classes: Wright–Fisher island model (n demes ∈ {2, 5, 20}, migration m ∈ [0.001, 0.5]); Moran process on cycles, regular graphs (degree 3–10) and random graphs with N ∈ {20, 50, 200}; two-player games with synergy d ∈ [−b, b]; and multiplicative versus additive fitness, at selection strengths δ from 10^-4 to 1. In each cell compute exactly (small N, linear algebra on the Markov chain) or by simulation with 10^6 replicates (larger N) the fixation probability of a single cooperator relative to neutral 1/N. Compare three predictors: parameter HR with model b, c and pedigree or identity-by-descent r; the weak-selection inclusive-fitness condition (Taylor–Frank); and regression HR, which holds by approach 1. Output the fraction of model space where parameter HR gives the right sign, as a function of δ and d.
steps: Implement exact Markov-chain fixation for small graphs and validated Monte Carlo for larger ones.
Pre-register the predictors and the agreement metric (sign agreement and, where nonzero, rank correlation of effect sizes).
Sweep the grid; publish the phase maps with code and seeds.
Identify the analytic boundary (for example agreement whenever d = 0 and δ → 0) and feed it back to approach 1 as a theorem to prove.
approaches.decisive_result: Phase maps showing, for each model class, the region where parameter-based r b > c correctly predicts the direction of selection. The pre-stated expectation is 100% agreement at d = 0, δ → 0, with measured degradation as |d| and δ grow; a region of disagreement at d = 0 under weak selection would itself be notable.
approaches.failure_signature: Monte Carlo noise at small fixation-probability differences makes signs undecidable in large parts of the grid (Wilson intervals overlapping 1/N), so the map is mostly 'unresolved'.

approaches.title: Computer-assisted proof of attractors via interval Newton and Conley–Morse graphs
approaches.method: Use the Atela–Golé–Hotton reduction: in the cylindrical hard-disk version of the Douady–Couder model (each new primordium at the lowest available position at distance ≥ D from existing ones on a cylinder of circumference 1), the dynamics reduce to a finite-dimensional map on 'fronts', the chains of most recent primordia. Rhombic lattices (Fibonacci, Lucas, bijugate and other parastichy pairs) are fixed points of this map up to translation. For the smooth-repulsion version (energy Σ exp(−|x − x_j|/λ) or a power law), the step map is piecewise smooth. Plan: (a) for each candidate branch (m, n), enclose the fixed point over parameter boxes in D (or Γ) with the interval Newton or Krawczyk operator in Arb/FLINT or CAPD, and enclose the Jacobian spectrum inside the unit disk to certify local attraction; (b) for global classification, build a Conley–Morse graph over a box grid of the reduced state space for each parameter box (the Arai et al. 2009 database method), certifying that every recurrent set is one of the enclosed fixed points; (c) the Lucas and bijugate branches enter as additional Morse sets with their own parameter ranges.
steps: Implement the front map exactly (hard-disk model) and the smooth-repulsion map; reproduce Douady–Couder bifurcation diagrams numerically.
Certify fixed points and stability with interval Newton or Krawczyk across D ∈ [D_min, 0.5] in boxes, adaptively refined.
Compute Conley–Morse graphs per parameter box; check that the Morse sets match the certified fixed points.
Publish the certified bifurcation diagram and code; describe precisely the parameter range covered.
approaches.decisive_result: A computer-assisted theorem: for all D in a stated range, the only attractors of the cylindrical front map are the certified lattice fixed points, which include the Fibonacci and Lucas branches with explicit ranges, and every other initial front converges to one of them. Basin boundaries are bounded by the Morse decomposition.
approaches.failure_signature: Conley–Morse graphs at feasible resolutions contain Morse sets that are not single fixed points (unresolved recurrent sets) in significant parameter ranges, or the discontinuities of the hard-disk map break the interval Newton enclosures near bifurcations.

approaches.title: Lean: lattice parastichy theorems from continued fractions
approaches.method: Formalize the static half of the theory, which every dynamical claim refers to and which is classical. For the lattice of points (kα mod 1, k·h), k ∈ ℤ, on a cylinder, with divergence α and rise h, prove: (a) the visible opposed parastichy pairs, the two shortest lattice vectors forming a basis and pointing in opposite directions, have numbers (q_j, q_{j+1}) given by consecutive denominators of convergents or intermediate fractions of α; (b) as h decreases, the visible pair changes exactly at the h-values where three vectors have equal length (triangular lattice points), and the sequence of pairs is the convergent sequence; (c) for α = the golden angle fraction (3 − √5)/2, all visible pairs are consecutive Fibonacci numbers, for α = 1/(3 + 1/φ) (the Lucas angle) consecutive Lucas numbers, and bijugate lattices give 2× Fibonacci pairs. Mathlib has generalized continued fractions (GenContFract) and Fibonacci (Nat.fib), so most groundwork exists.
steps: Define the cylindrical lattice, visible parastichy pairs and the shortest-vector basis in Lean.
Prove the convergent characterization using Mathlib's continued-fraction API and best-approximation lemmas.
Specialize to golden, Lucas and bijugate cases; prove the Fibonacci and Lucas statements.
Write a report linking each theorem to Thompson's ch14 claims in the repo.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module proving that the visible opposed parastichy numbers of the golden-angle lattice are consecutive Fibonacci numbers for every rise h, with the Lucas and bijugate analogues. It does not classify dynamical attractors, but certifies the lattice side that approach 1's fixed points are identified by.
approaches.failure_signature: Mathlib's best-approximation lemmas for continued fractions are not in the form needed, and proving them from scratch exceeds the time budget.

approaches.title: Simulated basin measures tested against citizen-science sunflower counts
approaches.method: Turn the model into a quantitative prediction about real plants. Simulate the Douady–Couder disc model and the cylindrical model over a slowly decreasing growth parameter Γ (the ontogenetic path from seedling to capitulum), starting from initial fronts sampled from a stated distribution (cotyledon arrangement: decussate or two-fold at stated rates, plus Gaussian positional noise σ ∈ {0.01, 0.03, 0.1}). Record the terminal parastichy pair class (Fibonacci, Lucas, double Fibonacci, other) and the basin measures with Wilson intervals from 10^5 runs per setting. Pre-register predicted class frequencies at each σ and compare with the Swinton et al. 2016 sunflower data and the repo's thompson1917-ch14-05/06 parastichy count tests, using a multinomial likelihood-ratio test. The pre-registered rule: the model supports the data if some σ in the grid gives p > 0.05 for the class distribution; it is refuted if all σ give p < 0.001 or if the model cannot produce the observed non-Fibonacci classes at all.
steps: Implement disc and cylinder simulators with an inhibition-field placement rule; validate against Douady and Couder 1996 diagrams.
Write result.json with predictions per σ and the decision rule before downloading the Swinton data.
Run 10^5 simulations per setting; estimate class frequencies.
Fetch the sunflower data, classify heads by published parastichy counts, run the multinomial test.
approaches.decisive_result: A pre-registered verdict on whether the Douady–Couder model, with one noise parameter, reproduces the observed frequencies of Fibonacci, Lucas and other classes in sunflowers. If it does, the basin measures are what the rigorous classification must explain.
approaches.failure_signature: Model frequencies cannot match the observed share of non-Fibonacci heads for any σ, or the data lack enough class detail to distinguish Lucas from other non-Fibonacci heads (then inconclusive, underpowered).

approaches.title: Pre-registered phylogenetic test of three quantitative predictions for the π–N slope
approaches.method: Extend Buffalo's (2021) compilation with independent census proxies from the organisms layer and state, before analysis, the slope each hypothesis predicts. Response: log₁₀ π at synonymous or neutral sites. Census proxy: log₁₀(range area × density), where range area is the convex hull or alpha hull of cleaned GBIF occurrences and density is predicted from body mass by Damuth's allometry (D ∝ M^−0.75), as Buffalo did, but with GBIF-derived ranges to test robustness. Predictions: (H0, neutral) slope of log π on log N_c ≈ 1 if N_e ∝ N_c and μ is constant; (H1, linked selection) slope reduced by the factor predicted from each species' map length and coding density using a Corbett-Detig-style model of background selection plus sweeps, computed per species before looking at π; (H2, demographic) π tracks the harmonic mean of population size, so slope ≈ 1 against harmonic-mean N but much less against current N_c. Fit PGLS with Pagel's λ (phylolm) on an Open Tree of Life synthetic tree with time calibration. Decision rule: H1 closes the gap if the observed slope lies within the 95% interval of the H1-predicted slope; H0 is refuted if the slope interval excludes 0.5.
steps: Write result.json with predicted slopes and intervals for H0, H1 and H2 before computing observed slopes.
Resolve species through the organisms layer; fetch GBIF occurrences with a cleaning pipeline (coordinate checks, outlier removal) and compute ranges.
Compute per-species predicted linked-selection reduction from published map lengths and genome annotations; record n for which inputs exist.
Fit PGLS; compare slopes; report residual orders of magnitude unexplained.
approaches.decisive_result: Observed PGLS slope with 95% CI compared against the pre-registered H0 and H1 intervals: the gap is closed if the observed slope falls in the H1 interval, and the residual is quantified in orders of magnitude otherwise. The minimum sample is 100 species with π and range; Buffalo's set is larger, so recombination-map availability limits only the H1 subset.
approaches.failure_signature: Census proxies from GBIF ranges and Damuth density have measurement error so large (or so correlated with body mass) that slope intervals overlap all three predictions: inconclusive, underpowered.

approaches.title: Decompose π into N_e and μ using pedigree mutation rates
approaches.method: Part of the paradox may sit in μ, not N_e: the drift-barrier hypothesis predicts that per-generation mutation rate falls as N_e rises, which flattens π = 4N_eμ against N_c. Pedigree-based germline mutation rates now exist for dozens of vertebrates (Bergeron et al. 2023). For every species with both a pedigree μ and a published π (Romiguier et al. 2014, Leffler et al. 2012, genome-scale estimates in NCBI-linked studies), compute N̂_e = π/(4μ) and fit log N̂_e on log N_c (PGLS). Pre-registered predictions: if the paradox is entirely in N_e, then log μ is uncorrelated with log N_c and the slope of log N̂_e equals the slope of log π; if drift-barrier compression matters, log μ declines with log N_c and the N̂_e slope is steeper than the π slope by the μ slope. The quantity of interest is the fraction of the gap between neutral slope 1 and the observed π slope that μ accounts for.
steps: Pre-register the decomposition and predicted signs; list admissible μ estimates (trio-based, with stated callable-genome correction).
Assemble the matched set (species with both μ and π); resolve taxa via the organisms layer.
Fit PGLS for log π, log μ and log N̂_e on log N_c; propagate μ uncertainty by parametric bootstrap.
Report the share of the paradox attributable to μ with its 95% interval.
approaches.decisive_result: The estimated slope of log μ on log N_c and the implied share of the π–N_c gap explained by mutation-rate variation, with 95% CI. If the share's interval excludes 0, μ is a quantified part of the answer; if it is centred near 0 with a tight interval, the paradox is entirely in N_e.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than about 30 species with both pedigree μ and comparable π, giving intervals spanning 0 to 100%: inconclusive, underpowered.

approaches.title: Simulation bound on how much linked selection can flatten π across N
approaches.method: Settle whether linked selection can close the gap by computing the most it could do under generous but empirically bounded parameters. Use SLiM forward simulation with tree-sequence recording plus msprime recapitation, and stdpopsim genome models and DFEs where available, across a ladder of census sizes N from 10^3 to 10^7 simulated directly. Extrapolate to 10^12 with the analytic background-selection and sweep formulas (B = exp(−Σ u/(s(1+r/s)²)) plus a recurrent-sweep coalescent rate), calibrated against the simulations in the overlap range. Upper-bound parameters: the deleterious mutation rate at the top of published estimates, a DFE fraction of strongly selected new mutations at the top of estimates, and adaptive substitution rate α from McDonald–Kreitman ranges. Output: the curve π(N) and the maximum achievable flattening (slope of log π on log N over 10^4–10^12). Compare with the observed slope from approach 1 or from Buffalo 2021.

Run SLiM simulations over the N ladder with 20 replicates each; compute π at neutral sites.
Calibrate the analytic B and sweep model to simulations; extrapolate to large N.
Compute the maximum flattening and compare with the observed slope.
approaches.decisive_result: The minimum π–N slope achievable by linked selection under upper-bound parameters. If that minimum exceeds the observed slope plus its CI, linked selection cannot explain the paradox, as Buffalo argued, and demography or μ must; if it falls below, the bound shows which parameter regime is needed.
approaches.failure_signature: Extrapolation from 10^7 to 10^12 is unreliable: the analytic model misfits simulations at the top of the ladder, or sweep interference (genetic draft saturation) makes predictions model-dependent across plausible formulas.

approaches.title: Pre-registered PGLS model comparison: single power law vs curvature vs clade slopes
approaches.method: Assemble mammal BMR and mass from AnAge (metabolic rate, body mass, body temperature fields) and PanTHERIA (BasalMetRate, AdultBodyMass), deduplicated by species via the organisms layer. Exclude records not meeting basal criteria where flagged, and require n ≥ 300 species with temperature for the temperature-corrected analysis. Models: (M1) log B = a + b log M; (M2) M1 + Boltzmann temperature term −E/(kT_b) (Gillooly form) or T_b as covariate; (M3) quadratic in log M (Kolokotrones curvature); (M4) order-level random slopes. Fit by PGLS with Pagel's λ, compare by AICc and by leave-one-order-out predictive log-likelihood. Pre-registered decision: 'single exponent' if M1 or M2 wins and the 95% CI of b excludes one of 2/3 or 3/4 (reported as such); 'no universal exponent' if M3 or M4 improves predictive log-likelihood by > 10 units summed over orders; 'underdetermined' if the CI contains both.

Download AnAge (dataset.zip) and PanTHERIA; record SHA-256; merge and resolve taxa.

approaches.title: Lean formalization of the WBE network derivation with the finite-size exponent
approaches.method: Make the disputed step explicit. Model: a branching network with N levels, branching ratio n, radius ratio β and length ratio γ per level, invariant terminal units (capillaries) and total blood volume V_b ∝ M. Define V_b(N) = Σ_{k=0}^{N} n^k π r_k² l_k with r_k = β^k r₀, l_k = γ^k l₀, so V_b = π r₀² l₀ Σ (nβ²γ)^k. Theorem 1 (exact finite form): with terminal size fixed, N_cap = n^N and V_b = V_cap · ((nβ²γ)^{−(N+1)} − 1)/((nβ²γ)^{−1} − 1) for nβ²γ < 1. Theorem 2 (asymptotic exponent): under area preservation β = n^{−1/2} and space filling γ = n^{−1/3}, and V_b ∝ M, the ratio log N_cap / log M → 3/4 as N → ∞, but for finite N the effective exponent is strictly less than 3/4 with an explicit correction term, matching Savage et al. 2008's finite-size analysis. Theorem 3: if area-preserving branching holds only below a transition level and Poiseuille scaling (β = n^{−1/3}) above it, the limiting exponent is different (explicit formula). The hypotheses V_b ∝ M and invariant terminal units are exactly where Kozłowski and Konarzewski object, and they appear as named hypotheses.
steps: Define the network sums in Lean (Finset.sum over levels, geometric series).
Prove Theorem 1 by geometric-series lemmas, and Theorem 2 by limits (Filter.Tendsto) on logarithms.
Prove Theorem 3 for the two-regime network.
Write a report with each hypothesis named and linked to Thompson's ch03-07 and ch02-01 claims; state which are empirical.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module proving that WBE's 3/4 is the N → ∞ limit under four named hypotheses, with the exact finite-N exponent, compiled with only standard axioms. Each published objection then corresponds to dropping a named hypothesis.
approaches.failure_signature: The formalization shows that the published derivation needs a hypothesis not listed (for example a specific relation between N and M) to get 3/4, which is a substantive finding about WBE rather than a failure, or the limit proofs in Mathlib take longer than budgeted.

approaches.title: Cross-domain heterogeneity test: one exponent across prokaryotes, protists and animals?
approaches.method: Universality claims cover all life, but approach 1 tests mammals. DeLong et al. 2010 compiled metabolic rates for prokaryotes, protists and metazoans and reported superlinear, approximately linear and sublinear exponents respectively. Re-analyse with a pre-registered hierarchical model: log B = a_g + b_g log M + temperature correction, with group g ∈ {prokaryotes, protists, ectothermic metazoans, endotherms}, b_g ~ Normal(b̄, τ²). Pre-registered decision: universality is refuted if τ's 95% posterior interval excludes 0.05 and at least two b_g intervals are disjoint; supported if τ < 0.03 and b̄'s interval contains 3/4 or 2/3. Add AnAge ectotherm entries with temperature to test whether temperature correction collapses ectotherm and endotherm slopes, as metabolic theory predicts.
steps: Pre-register the model, priors and decision thresholds.
Retrieve DeLong et al. 2010 supplementary data; add AnAge ectotherm records with temperature.
Fit the hierarchical model (Stan or PyMC) with measurement-error terms on M where reported.
Report τ, group slopes and the verdict; check sensitivity to the temperature correction.
approaches.decisive_result: The posterior for between-group slope heterogeneity τ, and whether group slopes overlap. Disjoint slopes across domains refute a single universal exponent regardless of the mammal result.
approaches.failure_signature: Group samples (especially prokaryotes and protists) too small or too heterogeneous in measurement protocol for slopes to be compared, leaving τ's interval wide: inconclusive, underpowered.

approaches.title: Pre-registered GBIF island SAR test with coverage-standardized richness
approaches.method: Archipelagos: Canary Islands, Galápagos, Hawaiian main islands, Azores, Balearic Islands, Cape Verde, chosen before looking at data because they have island areas in GIFT and dense GBIF sampling. Resolve island polygons and areas from GIFT; download GBIF occurrences per island polygon with a fetch script and checksums.
Compute coverage-standardized richness (and GIFT checklist richness for plants).
Fit all models with sars; compute AICc ranks and z intervals; apply the decision rule.

approaches.title: Sampling-only null: do lognormal SADs and random placement reproduce z?
approaches.method: Before asking what mechanism sets z ≈ 0.25, establish what z distribution arises with no mechanism beyond the species-abundance distribution and random placement. Preston (1962) and later May argued that a canonical lognormal yields z ≈ 0.26 for isolates. Compute this exactly over the range of conditions in real datasets. For each of a grid of total individuals J (10^3–10^9), species pools S₀ and SAD shapes (lognormal with σ ∈ [1, 3], log-series with α ∈ [5, 500], and Preston's canonical constraint), place individuals on islands proportional to area (Coleman random placement, expected richness E[S(a)] = Σ_i 1 − (1 − a)^{n_i}). Fit z over island-area spans matching each dataset in the Triantis et al. compilation (area range, number of islands), producing the null distribution of z per dataset. Compare the observed z distribution with the null by quantile regression and a two-sample Anderson–Darling test.
steps: Pre-register the SAD families, parameter grid and comparison statistics.
Compute expected richness curves analytically (Coleman formula) and stochastically for small J.
Match null conditions to each published dataset's area span and island count; generate null z.
Compare observed and null z distributions; report the variance in z the null explains.
approaches.decisive_result: The fraction of the between-dataset variance in z explained by SAD shape and area span alone. If the sampling null reproduces the observed z distribution (Anderson–Darling p > 0.05 under a plausible SAD), z ≈ 0.25 needs no ecological mechanism; if observed z is systematically higher (for example on isolated archipelagos), the excess quantifies the mechanism's contribution.
approaches.failure_signature: The null z depends so strongly on unobservable SAD parameters that a plausible SAD can be found to fit any observed z, so the null has no discriminating power.

approaches.title: Random-effects meta-analysis of z heterogeneity plus a METE scaling-collapse test
approaches.method: Universality means the true between-dataset variance τ² of z is near zero after sampling error. Using the Triantis et al. 2012 and Drakare et al. 2006 compilations, estimate each dataset's z with its standard error (refitting from the raw S–A data where supplied, otherwise from reported fits) and fit a random-effects meta-regression: z_j = μ + x_j'β + u_j + e_j, with u_j ~ N(0, τ²), e_j ~ N(0, se_j²), and covariates for isolation, island type, taxon and body size. Pre-registered: universality refuted if τ's 95% CI excludes 0.03, a z standard deviation one eighth of the canonical 0.25. Independently, test METE's specific prediction (Harte et al. 2009) that the local slope z at a scale is a universal decreasing function of log(N/S) at that scale: for datasets with abundance N, compute local slopes and test the collapse onto the METE curve by its residual variance against a free-curve alternative.
steps: Pre-register τ threshold, covariates and the METE collapse statistic.
Extract per-dataset z and SE; flag datasets with abundance data for the METE test.
Fit the random-effects meta-regression (REML) and report τ², I² and covariate effects.
Run the METE collapse test on datasets with abundances; report the residual variance ratio.
approaches.decisive_result: τ with CI (universality supported if the CI upper bound is < 0.03, refuted if the lower bound is > 0.03), the share of heterogeneity explained by covariates, and whether local slopes collapse onto the METE curve, the decisive test between 'universal exponent' and 'universal non-power form'.
approaches.failure_signature: Too few datasets report abundances for the METE test (fewer than 20), and z standard errors are unavailable for most compiled curves, making τ uninterpretable.

approaches.title: Pre-registered PBDB test: hat-shapedness of subsampled trajectories versus an MBL null
approaches.method: Download PBDB occurrences at genus resolution for all orders and families, assign occurrences to stages (ICS 2023), and estimate per-stage richness by shareholder quorum subsampling at quorum 0.7 (divDyn). Include clades with ≥ 6 stages of duration and ≥ 50 occurrences. Hat-shapedness statistics: (a) center of gravity CG ∈ [0, 1] of the subsampled diversity curve (Gould et al. 1987); (b) a unimodality score, the share of total variation explained by the best single-peaked isotonic fit; (c) a symmetry score |CG − 0.5|. Null: the Raup et al. (1973) MBL process, a homogeneous birth–death process with per-clade origination and extinction rates estimated from the clade's own boundary-crosser counts, conditioned on clade duration and terminal diversity, passed through the same sampling (per-stage sampling probabilities from three-timer analysis) and the same SQS procedure. Pre-registered verdict: hat-shape is a real pattern if the fraction of clades with unimodality above the null's 95th percentile exceeds 5% by at least 10 percentage points (binomial test p < 0.01).
steps: Write result.json with inclusion thresholds, statistics, null and decision rule before downloading.
Fetch PBDB occurrences via the API with a scripted query; record checksums.
Compute SQS curves per clade; compute CG, unimodality and symmetry.
Simulate 1,000 null clades per real clade; compute empirical percentiles; apply the decision rule; report effect sizes separately for marine invertebrates and terrestrial vertebrates.
approaches.decisive_result: The fraction of clades significantly hat-shaped against a sampling-matched birth–death null, with its binomial CI. Reaching that fraction is the effect size the problem asks for. Several hundred qualifying families are expected, enough to detect a 10-point excess.
approaches.failure_signature: The null's percentiles are dominated by the conditioning on duration and terminal diversity (conditioned random walks are themselves hat-shaped), leaving no power to detect an excess; or SQS fails for many clades with low occurrence counts.

approaches.title: Model-based rates: does net diversification decline through clade life?
approaches.method: Hat-shapedness from diversity curves is indirect; the mechanistic claim (Quental and Marshall) is that origination falls and extinction rises with clade age. Estimate this directly with PyRate (Bayesian joint estimation of preservation, origination and extinction from occurrence data) for each family with ≥ 20 genera and ≥ 100 occurrences, using a time-variable preservation model. For each clade compute the posterior of the slope of net diversification rate r(t) = λ(t) − μ(t) against standardized clade age (birth–death shift model or a linear-trend model in clade age). Pre-registered: the claim holds if more than 50% of clades have posterior probability > 0.95 of a negative slope, and the median slope is negative with a 95% interval excluding 0; it fails if negative-slope clades are no more frequent than positive-slope ones.
steps: Pre-register clade inclusion, PyRate settings (preservation model, MCMC length, convergence criteria ESS > 200) and the decision rule.
Prepare PyRate inputs from PBDB occurrences with age ranges.
Run PyRate per clade on a compute cluster; check convergence.
Summarize slope posteriors across clades; apply the decision rule; compare with approach 1's CG and unimodality.
approaches.decisive_result: The distribution across clades of the posterior slope of net diversification versus clade age. A majority of significantly negative slopes would support Red-Queen decline as general; a symmetric distribution around zero would mean hat shapes, if present, are not driven by systematic rate decline.
approaches.failure_signature: Rate trends are not identifiable from preservation trends for most clades (posterior slopes span zero widely), which is likely for small clades: inconclusive.

approaches.title: Artifact audit: hat-shape from Linnaean grouping and the pull of the recent
approaches.method: Critics attribute symmetric clade histories to how clades are defined. Measure that directly. Simulate phylogenies under homogeneous birth–death (no rate decline) for 10^4 replicates per parameter set spanning observed origination and extinction rates. Partition each tree into named 'taxa' with three rules: (a) monophyletic crown and stem clades; (b) a Linnaean-style rule that founds a new 'family' when morphological divergence (Brownian character) passes a threshold, leaving paraphyletic remainders, as taxonomists do; (c) rank-by-age cuts. Apply realistic fossil sampling (Poisson preservation with rates from PBDB three-timer estimates) and the pull of the recent (perfect sampling of extant taxa). Compute the same CG and unimodality statistics as approach 1. The artifact share is the excess hat-shapedness under (b) and under the pull of the recent relative to (a) with uniform sampling. Then test on real data: restrict approach 1 to clades whose monophyly is supported in Open Tree of Life and to wholly extinct clades, and compare effect sizes.
steps: Implement birth–death simulation with character evolution and the three taxon-definition rules.
Add preservation and pull-of-the-recent sampling; compute hat statistics per pseudo-taxon.
Quantify artifact contributions per rule; publish code and seeds.
Rerun approach 1 on monophyletic-only and extinct-only subsets; compare with the simulated artifact sizes.
approaches.decisive_result: The amount of hat-shapedness (excess unimodality over the MBL null) produced by paraphyletic definition and the pull of the recent in simulations with no real decline, compared with the excess in real data. If real excess ≤ simulated artifact excess, the pattern is an artifact; if real monophyletic and extinct-only clades retain the excess, it is not.
approaches.failure_signature: The Linnaean rule cannot be calibrated: artifact size depends on an arbitrary divergence threshold over the plausible range, so the comparison has no fixed reference.

approaches.title: Measure Raup parameters from 3D scans and compare occupancy models on held-out taxa
approaches.method: Build the dataset the field lacks. From MorphoSource CT and surface scans of gastropod, ammonoid (where 3D fossil scans exist) and bivalve shells, and iDigBio 2D images in standard apertural view for gastropods, extract the coiling axis and the generating-curve centroid trajectory, and fit Raup's W (whorl expansion per revolution), D (relative distance of generating curve from axis) and T (translation) by nonlinear least squares on the spiral. Fit generating-curve shape with elliptic Fourier coefficients. Use the morpholib MorphoEval pipeline for segmentation and quality scoring, and admit a specimen only if fit RMSE < 3% of shell height. Target: ≥ 500 species across ≥ 50 families, taxa resolved via the organisms layer and MolluscaBase. Occupancy models over (log W, D, T): (M_dev) a developmental-constraint density proportional to the volume of parameter space producing geometrically valid, non-self-intersecting shells, with correlations imposed by the generating curve; (M_fun) density decreasing with distance below functional thresholds, from approach 2; (M_phy) phylogenetic Brownian or OU model on the molluscan tree with no boundaries; and combinations. Score by predictive log-likelihood on held-out families (leave-one-family-out).
steps: Pre-register specimen admission criteria, models and the held-out scoring rule.
Query MorphoSource and iDigBio for shell media; build the fetch list with licences and checksums.
Run segmentation and spiral fitting through morpholib; quality-filter.
Fit the occupancy models; compute held-out log-likelihood; produce the empty-region map under the winning model.
approaches.decisive_result: A ranked comparison of developmental, functional and phylogenetic occupancy models by held-out predictive log-likelihood (a difference > 10 units counts as decisive), plus a map of the empty region with the winning model's predicted boundary.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than about 200 species pass quality filters, or no model beats the phylogenetic random walk on held-out families, which is the problem's stated falsifier.

approaches.title: Compute functional landscapes over the whole Raup space by generative modelling and FE
approaches.method: Make the functional hypothesis predictive before looking at occupancy. Generate shells on a dense grid over (log W ∈ [0, 6], D ∈ [0, 0.9], T ∈ [0, 6]) with a circular or elliptical generating curve. For each, compute: (a) internal volume per unit shell material (constructional economy); (b) for planispiral forms, hydrostatic stability, the distance between centres of buoyancy and mass with a stated tissue density; (c) crushing resistance by linear-elastic finite-element analysis of a compression load across the aperture, normalized by material volume; (d) a self-overlap indicator (whorls that would intersect). Define the functional hypothesis as the Pareto front of (a)–(c). Its predicted occupied region is the set of points within δ of the front, with δ fixed from a pilot of 20 species chosen at random and excluded from approach 1's test. The output is a predicted occupancy surface supplied to approach 1 as M_fun.
steps: Implement the Raup generator with mesh output; validate against published Raup figures.
Compute volume and material metrics analytically or numerically on the grid.
Run FE compression on a coarser grid (about 10^4 shells) and interpolate.
Compute the Pareto front and the predicted occupancy surface; freeze it before approach 1's scoring.
approaches.decisive_result: A pre-computed functional occupancy surface whose boundary is fixed before occupancy data are examined, evaluated in approach 1 against developmental and phylogenetic surfaces. If it predicts the empty regions (for example sparse occupancy at high D and low W), functional selection is supported quantitatively.
approaches.failure_signature: The Pareto front is so broad that nearly the whole space is within δ, so it predicts no empty region, or results are dominated by the arbitrary choice of load case.

approaches.title: Lean-proved constructional boundaries of Raup space plus a growth-rule reachability map
approaches.method: Separate what geometry forbids outright from what development or selection disfavours. Formalize in Lean the logarithmic-spiral shell: the generating curve's centroid at angle θ is at radius r(θ) = r₀ W^{θ/2π}, with the curve's inner edge at distance proportional to D·r. Prove: (a) successive whorls just touch when D = 1/W, Raup's boundary between overlapping and separated coils, generalized to elliptical generating curves; (b) a whorl penetrates the previous one exactly when D < 1/W under stated conditions, with the conditions on T for helicospiral forms; (c) for T = 0, an umbilicus exists iff D > 0. These carve out the constructionally impossible region (self-intersection), which must not count as an 'unexplained empty region'. Second, derive developmental reachability from local aperture growth rules (Moulton–Goriely style, with growth rate varying around the aperture): compute which (W, D, T) combinations are produced by growth-rate profiles in a bounded family, giving the developmental-constraint surface M_dev for approach 1.
steps: Define the spiral shell in Lean with ℝ parameters; prove the touching and penetration conditions with explicit hypotheses.
Report the theorems against Thompson ch11 claims (logarithmic spiral generative model).
Implement an aperture-growth model; sample growth-rate profiles; record resulting (W, D, T).
Produce the reachability density as M_dev for approach 1.
approaches.decisive_result: Lean theorems giving the exact self-intersection boundary of Raup space (D = 1/W and its elliptical and helicospiral generalizations), and a growth-rule reachability density. Together they separate 'impossible', 'developmentally unlikely' and 'possible but unoccupied' regions, the three-way distinction the problem needs.
approaches.failure_signature: The growth-rule family is so flexible that every geometrically valid point is reachable, leaving M_dev uninformative; or the geometric theorems hold only under circular generating curves, too restrictive for real gastropods.
