approaches.title: Pre-registered test: clock period and PSM dynamics versus vertebral counts
approaches.method: Avoid the tautology. 'One somite per clock cycle' makes N = (duration of somitogenesis)/(period) trivially true, so the test must predict N from quantities measured independently of the count: the clock period τ, the rate at which the presomitic mesoderm (PSM) is replenished by the tailbud, and the PSM length at onset, which together determine when the PSM is exhausted (Gomez et al. 2008). Compile from time-lapse literature every species with τ and PSM dynamics measured: zebrafish, medaka, chick, mouse, corn snake, and human and other mammals from in vitro PSM systems (Matsuda et al. 2020), at stated temperatures. Predict total somite number N̂ from the Gomez-type balance model with parameters measured, not fitted. Compare with observed somite or vertebral counts from literature and museum data via the organisms layer (FishBase for fish vertebrae; Head and Polly 2015 for squamates). Pre-registered tolerance: supports if |N̂ − N|/N ≤ 15% in every species with complete data; refutes if > 30% in two or more.
steps: Write result.json with the prediction formula, tolerance and admissible measurement types.
Compile τ, PSM length and elongation rates per species with temperature; record sources.
Compute N̂ and compare with observed counts.

Compute, for unmeasured species, the expected reduction in posterior uncertainty about the mechanism from measuring τ (value-of-information ranking), using the variance of predicted N across plausible τ.
approaches.decisive_result: Per-species predicted versus observed somite numbers within or outside the 15% tolerance for all species with independent measurements (n ≈ 5–8), plus a ranked list of species whose clock measurement would most reduce uncertainty: long-bodied fishes, caecilians, and snakes other than corn snake.
approaches.failure_signature: Too few species have PSM dynamics measured independently of somite counts (n < 4), so the test is underpowered; or published measurements were taken at temperatures incompatible with the counts.

approaches.title: Fit a PSM balance model across species and predict held-out species
approaches.method: Formalize the clock-and-wavefront count as a dynamical model and test it out of sample. Model: PSM length L(t) obeys dL/dt = v_g(t) − v_s(t), where v_g is tailbud addition and v_s = S(t)/τ(t) is segmentation (segment length S over period τ), with S set by the wavefront speed, S = v_w τ. Somitogenesis ends at t* when L(t*) = L_min. N = ∫₀^{t*} dt/τ(t). Prove in Lean the qualitative theorems: (a) with constant τ and v_g decaying exponentially at rate k, N is an explicit closed-form function of τ k and L₀/S₀; (b) N increases when τ decreases at fixed elongation and v_w (the snake mechanism), and the elasticity of N to τ is exactly −1 only when elongation is independent of the clock. Then fit the free parameters (k and L_min) on four well-measured species and predict N for a held-out fifth (leave-one-out), comparing elasticity predictions with snake–lizard contrasts.

Extract L(t), S(t) and τ(t) from published time courses (zebrafish, chick, mouse, corn snake).
Fit k and L_min; predict the held-out species; report leave-one-out errors.
State which comparative contrast (for example snake versus lizard) would most sharply test the elasticity prediction.
approaches.decisive_result: Leave-one-out prediction errors for N across the measured species (decisive if all within 15%), and a Lean-proved elasticity statement making precise how much of the snake's high count is due to τ versus elongation.
approaches.failure_signature: Leave-one-out errors exceed 30% for any species, meaning species differ in mechanisms the model lacks (for example termination by Hox or Gdf11 timing rather than PSM depletion).

approaches.title: Temperature test: do clock and elongation Q10s predict meristic plasticity?
approaches.method: Use temperature as a natural perturbation the swarm can exploit from existing data. In ectotherms, temperature changes both clock period and elongation rate. Clock-and-wavefront predicts that total somite number varies with rearing temperature in proportion to the difference of their thermal sensitivities: d ln N / dT ≈ (E_τ − E_elong)/(kT²) in Arrhenius form. If both scale identically, N is temperature-invariant, as reported for zebrafish somitogenesis by Schröter et al. 2008. Compile (a) clock-period and elongation-rate temperature series for zebrafish and any other species with them, and (b) laboratory rearing-temperature experiments reporting vertebral counts in fishes (meristic plasticity literature), plus (c) the latitudinal vertebral-count gradient (Jordan's rule) from FishBase across species and populations. Pre-registered predictions: the measured E difference predicts the sign and magnitude of rearing-temperature effects within a factor of 2, and species whose measured E difference is near zero show no latitudinal gradient.
steps: Pre-register the Arrhenius prediction and tolerance.
Extract temperature series for τ and elongation from published studies; estimate E values with CIs.
Compile rearing-temperature vertebral-count experiments; compute d ln N/dT per study.
Compare predicted and observed slopes; run a phylogenetically controlled test of Jordan's rule against predicted sensitivity where data allow.
approaches.decisive_result: Agreement or disagreement, within a factor of 2, between d ln N/dT predicted from measured clock and elongation thermal sensitivities and the observed rearing-temperature effect on vertebral counts. A sign mismatch in two or more species refutes the clock-and-wavefront account of meristic plasticity.

approaches.title: Pre-registered multi-tissue branching-exponent estimation with errors-in-variables
approaches.method: Datasets: retinal fundus segmentations (DRIVE, HRF, manual vessel annotations), whole mouse brain vasculature (VesSAP), pig coronary morphometry (Kassab et al. 1993 tables) and xylem conduit data (McCulloh et al. 2003). At each bifurcation estimate radii from the segmentation distance transform averaged over a segment length of 5–10 radii away from the junction, and solve r₀^x = r₁^x + r₂^x for x by root-finding. Estimate per-tissue exponent distributions with a hierarchical errors-in-variables model: observed radii are true radii plus heteroscedastic noise with variance calibrated from approach 3. Hypotheses, stated in advance: H3, x = 3 (Murray); H7/3, x = 7/3 (turbulent, large arteries); H_none, no single x across tissues (between-tissue SD of x > 0.3). Decision: a tissue supports H3 if the 95% interval of its mean x contains 3 and excludes 7/3; it supports H7/3 conversely; H_none holds if tissue intervals are disjoint. Also test shear dependence: x versus vessel diameter class within retina and brain.
steps: Write result.json with datasets, estimator, noise calibration source and decision rules.
Download DRIVE and HRF; obtain VesSAP graphs; transcribe Kassab and McCulloh tables; record checksums.
Extract bifurcations and radii; fit the hierarchical model with noise priors from approach 3.
Report per-tissue x intervals, the diameter-class trend and the verdict.
approaches.decisive_result: Per-tissue posterior intervals for the branching exponent across at least four tissue types, and a verdict among x = 3, x = 7/3, or no single exponent. Thousands of bifurcations per dataset give intervals of about ±0.1 once measurement error is modelled.
approaches.failure_signature: Calibrated measurement noise in image-derived radii (2D retinal images especially) inflates x intervals beyond ±0.5, so 3 and 7/3 cannot be distinguished: inconclusive, measurement-limited.

approaches.title: Lean formalization of Murray's cubic law and its turbulent and load-bearing variants
approaches.method: Formalize the optimization so that each empirical exponent has a precise theoretical antecedent. Cost per unit length of a vessel with flow Q and radius r: C(r) = 8μQ²/(πr⁴) + b π r², Poiseuille dissipation plus metabolic maintenance proportional to volume. Theorem 1: C has a unique minimizer on r > 0, with r³ = (16μ/(bπ²))^{1/2} · Q, so Q ∝ r³. Theorem 2: with flow conservation Q₀ = Q₁ + Q₂ at a bifurcation and each segment at its optimum, r₀³ = r₁³ + r₂³. Theorem 3 (turbulent): with dissipation ∝ Q^{7/4}r^{−19/4} (Blasius friction), optimal radius r ∝ Q^{3/7}, giving exponent 7/3 at bifurcations. Theorem 4 (xylem): if conduits also bear mechanical load with cost ∝ r² independent of flow, the optimum shifts away from the cubic law (explicit exponent), matching McCulloh et al.'s observation that load-bearing conduits deviate. Proofs use derivative sign analysis (Mathlib's deriv and monotonicity lemmas) and rpow algebra.
steps: Define the cost functions with ℝ and positivity hypotheses.
Prove existence, uniqueness and the closed form of the minimizer (first-derivative test, strict convexity).
Derive bifurcation exponents for laminar and turbulent cases with flow conservation.
Report each theorem linked to thompson1917-ch15-13 with scope notes on what data must decide.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module proving the cubic law, the 7/3 turbulent law and the load-bearing deviation from explicit cost functions, compiled with only standard axioms. This makes approach 1's hypotheses theorem-backed.
approaches.failure_signature: None mathematically. The risk is rpow manipulations in Mathlib taking longer than expected; low risk.

approaches.title: Synthetic-tree calibration: can image-derived radii distinguish exponent 3 from 7/3?
approaches.method: Exponent estimates from images are biased: estimating x from r₀^x = r₁^x + r₂^x is nonlinear, and radius noise near junctions inflates or deflates x. Before trusting approach 1, generate synthetic vascular trees with known exponent x_true ∈ {2, 7/3, 2.7, 3}, using constrained constructive optimization or a simple binary tree with stated asymmetry and length ratios. Render them through realistic image formation for each modality: a fundus model (2D projection, Gaussian blur, vessel central reflex, noise at matched SNR); light-sheet volumes for VesSAP (anisotropic PSF, voxel size); micro-CT. Run the same segmentation and radius pipeline as approach 1. Output: the bias and variance of estimated x as a function of x_true, vessel size in pixels and modality. These become the noise priors in approach 1's model, and determine the minimum vessel diameter (in pixels) at which 3 and 7/3 are distinguishable.
steps: Implement the synthetic tree generator and modality-specific forward image models.
Run approach 1's segmentation pipeline on 10^3 synthetic trees per setting.
Fit bias and variance curves for x as functions of x_true and diameter in pixels.
Publish calibration tables; set approach 1's minimum-diameter inclusion threshold from them.
approaches.decisive_result: Calibration curves giving, for each modality, the smallest vessel diameter at which estimated x separates 3 from 7/3 with 95% power. If no real dataset reaches that resolution, approach 1 is underpowered by design and the question needs better imaging.
approaches.failure_signature: Forward models fail validation: synthetic images differ visibly from real ones in vessel-contrast statistics, so the calibration does not transfer.

approaches.title: Matched permutation test of GO/HPO morphogenesis–learning overlap via INDRA CoGEx
approaches.method: Gene sets: M = human genes annotated (experimental evidence codes only, to limit annotation-cascade bias) to GO 'anatomical structure morphogenesis' (GO:0009653) or descendants, or to HPO 'abnormality of body morphology'-type branches; L = genes annotated to GO 'learning or memory' (GO:0007611) or descendants, or to HPO memory and learning phenotypes. Retrieve via INDRA CoGEx (GO and HPO edges are in the graph). Statistic: observed |M ∩ L| over the expected value under a matched null. Null: 10^5 permutations drawing gene sets of the same sizes in which each gene is replaced by a random gene from the same stratum of (number of distinct GO biological-process annotations: pleiotropy, in deciles; publication count from CoGEx literature edges: annotation bias, in deciles; GTEx expression breadth τ: housekeeping, in tertiles). Pre-registered 'wide overlap': observed/expected ≥ 1.5 with permutation p < 0.001. Refuted: observed/expected ≤ 1.1 or p > 0.05. Repeat on the bioelectric subset (ion channels and gap junctions: HGNC groups for voltage-gated channels, K2P, connexins, innexins, pannexins).
steps: Write result.json with GO and HPO identifiers, evidence-code filter, strata, threshold and the bioelectric subset definition.
Query INDRA CoGEx for annotations and publication counts; fetch GTEx breadth; record query hashes.
Run the stratified permutation test for all genes and for the bioelectric subset.
Compare with the repo's existing levin-2022-tame-19 verdict and record a revision if the verdict changes.
approaches.decisive_result: Observed/expected overlap with permutation p under a null matched for pleiotropy, annotation depth and expression breadth, for all genes and for ion-channel and gap-junction genes, with pre-registered thresholds for 'wide overlap'.
approaches.failure_signature: Strata are so collinear (highly studied genes are also highly pleiotropic and broadly expressed) that the matched null has too few genes per stratum to permute, making p-values unstable.

approaches.title: Annotation-independent test using mouse knockout phenotyping (IMPC/MGI)
approaches.method: GO and HPO overlap inherits curation bias. The International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium phenotypes knockouts systematically through a fixed pipeline, so which genes are tested for which phenotypes does not depend on prior interest. For all IMPC knockout lines that completed both morphological (skeletal, craniofacial, organ morphology) and behavioural or neurological procedures, build a 2 × 2 table: abnormal morphology yes/no versus abnormal learning-related or behavioural phenotype yes/no. Fit logistic regression of the behavioural call on the morphology call with covariates: number of other phenotype systems hit (pleiotropy), viability class and sex. Supplement with MGI curated knockouts restricted to studies reporting both kinds. Pre-registered: an adjusted odds ratio ≥ 2 (95% CI excluding 1.3) supports a shared gene set beyond pleiotropy; OR CI including 1 refutes it. Run the ion-channel and gap-junction subset separately.
steps: Pre-register phenotype term sets (MP ontology IDs), covariates and thresholds.
Download IMPC statistical results; filter to lines with both procedure classes; record version and checksums.
Fit adjusted logistic models for all genes and the bioelectric subset.
Compare with approach 1 to see whether annotation-based and screen-based answers agree.
approaches.decisive_result: An adjusted odds ratio, with CI, for co-occurrence of morphological and behavioural or learning phenotypes in systematically phenotyped knockouts. This is the strongest available test free of curation bias.
approaches.failure_signature: IMPC behavioural procedures measure activity and anxiety rather than learning per se, so the 'learning' category cannot be operationalized; the test then reverts to a broader behavioural proxy, which must be stated as a reinterpretation.

approaches.title: Mechanistic proximity: network separation of the two modules in INDRA's causal graph
approaches.method: Overlap counts shared members. TAME's claim is better read as shared machinery: the modules may be mechanistically adjacent without sharing genes. Use the network separation s_AB = ⟨d_AB⟩ − (⟨d_AA⟩ + ⟨d_BB⟩)/2 of Menche et al. 2015, computed on INDRA CoGEx's causal statement graph between human genes (indra_rel edges with evidence_count ≥ 2, undirected for distance). A = core morphogenesis set and B = core learning/memory set (experimental GO annotations), with SynGO synaptic genes as a positive-control module expected to be near B. Null: degree-preserving randomization, sampling gene sets with matched degree distribution (binned), 10^4 draws. Pre-registered: s_AB < 0 with z < −3 against the degree-matched null supports shared machinery; s_AB ≥ 0 refutes it. Repeat after removing the top 1% highest-degree hubs to check that shared housekeeping hubs do not drive proximity.
steps: Pre-register edge filters, gene sets, null and thresholds.
Export the INDRA causal subgraph via execute_cypher; record the query and statement-hash counts.
Compute s_AB and the null distribution; run the hub-removal sensitivity check.
For gene pairs driving proximity, cite INDRA statement hashes and PMIDs as mechanistic evidence.
approaches.decisive_result: Network separation s_AB with z-score against a degree-matched null, with and without hubs. Negative separation surviving hub removal would support Levin's shared-machinery prediction in a form the overlap test cannot detect; non-negative separation would refute it.
approaches.failure_signature: INDRA's causal graph is so dominated by literature-heavy genes that degree matching cannot remove study bias (separation tracks publication count), so the result reflects literature structure rather than biology.

approaches.title: Curated Vmem image corpus and a decoder validated by leave-one-study-out
approaches.method: Build an image corpus from open-access Levin-lab and other papers showing voltage-reporter dye images (DiBAC4(3), CC2-DMPE:DiSBAC2(3)) of control and perturbed Xenopus embryos and planarian fragments, each linked to the reported anatomical outcome class: for Xenopus craniofacial or eye, normal, ectopic eye, malformed face; for planaria, one head, two heads, no head. Register images to a common template (embryo outline or fragment axis), extract a low-dimensional Vmem feature vector (template-aligned intensity on a coarse grid, normalized to within-image range because dye images are not absolutely calibrated). Train simple, pre-registered decoders (multinomial logistic regression on 20 PCA components; k-NN) and evaluate leave-one-study-out, so test images come from papers not used in training. Pre-registered success: balanced accuracy ≥ 0.70 against a chance level computed from class frequencies, permutation p < 0.01.
steps: Pre-register inclusion criteria (open licence, dye named, outcome reported for the imaged individual or the imaged group), decoder, features and threshold.
Harvest figures with their licences; annotate outcome labels from the papers' text; record provenance.
Register images and extract features via the morpholib pipeline where applicable.
Run leave-one-study-out evaluation and the permutation test; report confusion matrices.
approaches.decisive_result: Leave-one-study-out balanced accuracy of anatomy-class prediction from Vmem images, against chance, with a permutation p-value. Above 0.70 supports a predictive mapping; at chance refutes the predictive form for those tissues.
approaches.failure_signature: Most published Vmem images show group-representative embryos without individual outcome labels, or too few studies (fewer than 5 per tissue) exist for leave-one-study-out: inconclusive, data-unavailable.

approaches.title: Pre-registered forward predictions of perturbation outcomes from bioelectric simulation
approaches.method: Test the instructive (causal) form of the hypothesis on perturbations whose outcomes are published but held out from calibration. Calibrate a BETSE or frontier_simulate model of the planarian fragment (ion channels, pumps, gap junctions per Durant et al. 2017 and Pietak and Levin 2017) on control and two perturbation conditions only. Then, for each held-out perturbation in the literature (for example ivermectin-induced hyperpolarization, SCH-28080 H,K-ATPase inhibition, octanol gap-junction block at stated concentrations), predict the steady-state anterior–posterior Vmem pattern. Map it to anatomy with a rule fixed in advance: a depolarized region above threshold θ predicts a head, θ fixed from the calibration conditions. Lodge predictions as a timestamped commit before comparison. Score the fraction of held-out perturbations whose predicted outcome class matches the published one, against a baseline that always predicts the most common outcome.
steps: Fix model structure and calibration conditions; pre-register the Vmem-to-anatomy rule and the held-out list.
Calibrate parameters on the calibration set; freeze.
Simulate each held-out perturbation; commit predictions before reading outcomes.
Compare with published outcomes; report accuracy against the baseline with a binomial test.
approaches.decisive_result: The fraction of held-out pharmacological and genetic perturbations whose anatomical outcome class the frozen model predicts, against the most-common-class baseline. Accuracy significantly above baseline (binomial p < 0.01, at least 10 held-out conditions) supports the predictive bioelectric code; baseline accuracy refutes this model's version of it.
approaches.failure_signature: Too few held-out perturbations with clear published outcomes and known molecular targets (fewer than 10), or model outcomes so sensitive to unmeasured parameters that predictions are not robust to plausible parameter ranges (report the fraction of the parameter posterior agreeing).

approaches.title: Dose–response meta-analysis: does Vmem shift size predict penetrance?
approaches.method: A predictive code implies graded dependence: larger, more localized Vmem shifts should give higher penetrance of the predicted phenotype. Code every published bioelectric perturbation experiment in Xenopus and planaria reporting both (a) a quantitative Vmem change (reporter intensity ratio or electrode mV, with dispersion) and (b) phenotype penetrance (k of n animals). Fit a random-effects logistic meta-regression of penetrance on the standardized Vmem shift, with study as a random effect and tissue and perturbation class (channel misexpression, drug, gap-junction block) as covariates. Pre-registered: a positive slope with 95% CI excluding 0, and the shift explaining ≥ 30% of between-condition variance, support the graded predictive form; a slope CI including 0 refutes it. Check small-study effects with funnel plots and Egger's test, since positive results may be preferentially published.
steps: Pre-register extraction rules, effect-size standardization and the model.
Systematically search open-access literature; double-extract data (two independent agents) and reconcile.
Fit the meta-regression; run publication-bias diagnostics.
Link each coded study to repo claims (levin-2018-hcn2, levin-2019-boundary) and record evidence.
approaches.decisive_result: The meta-regression slope of phenotype penetrance on Vmem shift magnitude with CI, and the variance explained, adjusted for publication bias.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 15 conditions report both a quantitative Vmem change and penetrance, or Egger's test shows strong small-study bias making the slope uninterpretable.

approaches.title: Re-run the Biswas protocol on 35 BioModels and ≥ 350 matched random ODE networks
approaches.method: Reimplement the Biswas et al. 2021 protocol: choose stimulus nodes (UCS, CS) and a response node, apply the stimulus schedules for each memory type (UCS-based, pairing, transfer, associative, consolidation) and score memory by the paper's criteria and thresholds. Validate by reproducing their per-model memory calls on the 35 BioModels models (agreement ≥ 90% required before proceeding). Null ensemble: for each biological model, generate 10 random networks matched on node count, edge count and density, in- and out-degree sequences (configuration model), kinetic forms (mass-action and Hill terms in the same proportions, with Hill coefficients drawn from the model's empirical distribution), parameter values drawn from the model's own log-parameter distribution, and stability (retain only networks with a stable steady state from the default initial condition, as biological models have). Simulate with libRoadRunner. Statistic: per memory type, the fraction of (network, stimulus/response triple) combinations showing memory, biological versus random. Pre-registered: 'biological signature' if the biological rate exceeds the random rate by ≥ 2× with a stratified permutation p < 0.01; 'generic' if the ratio is ≤ 1.2.
steps: Reimplement the protocol; validate against the paper's reported calls; publish the discrepancy list.
Write result.json with matching criteria, statistic and thresholds before simulating random networks.
Generate ≥ 350 matched random networks; check matching statistics.
Run all protocols; compute rates and ratios with stratified permutation p-values; publish code and seeds.
approaches.decisive_result: Per memory type, the ratio of memory rates in biological versus matched random networks with permutation p. A ratio ≥ 2 supports the biological-signature reading and ≤ 1.2 supports 'generic nonlinear dynamics', which is the problem's stated falsifier.
approaches.failure_signature: Reproduction of the original calls falls below 90% agreement because protocol details are underspecified in the paper, so any comparison tests a different protocol.

approaches.title: Attribution by surgery: rewire topology vs shuffle parameters in real models
approaches.method: Random networks differ from biological ones in many ways at once. A sharper design perturbs the biological models themselves along one axis at a time. For each of the 35 models: (a) topology surgery, degree-preserving edge swaps (100 swaps per edge) keeping every reaction's rate law and parameters; (b) parameter surgery, permuting parameter values among reactions of the same kinetic type, keeping topology; (c) kinetic surgery, replacing Hill terms with Michaelis–Menten terms (n = 1), keeping topology and parameters; (d) a combination. Generate 20 variants per model per surgery, discard variants without a stable steady state, and re-run the memory protocol. Memory that survives (a) but not (b) points to tuned parameters; memory surviving (b) but lost under (c) points to cooperativity (ultrasensitivity) as the generic cause. This decomposes any biological enrichment from approach 1 into causes.
steps: Implement SBML-level surgery operators with libsbml; verify that variants remain valid and stable.
Pre-register the attribution logic (which surgery outcomes imply which cause).
Run the memory protocol on all variants.
Report per-memory-type retention rates under each surgery with CIs.
approaches.decisive_result: Retention rates of each memory type under topology, parameter and kinetic surgery. For example, '80% of UCS memory survives topology rewiring but only 20% survives replacing Hill terms' would identify ultrasensitivity, not network wiring, as the cause.
approaches.failure_signature: Most surgical variants lose steady-state stability, so the surviving variants are a biased subset and retention rates are uninterpretable.

approaches.title: Theory: memory as multistability or slow manifolds, predicted by CRNT
approaches.method: Explain which networks can show which memory, so the result is a theorem plus a prediction rather than only a rate comparison. Step 1 (proof): show that, for the protocol's definitions, persistent UCS-based memory over a test window T after stimulus removal requires either (i) multistability, with the stimulus switching basins, or (ii) a slow variable with relaxation time ≥ T. The argument: if the system is monostable with all eigenvalues at the steady state having real part ≤ −λ and the steady state is globally attracting with exponential rate λ, the response returns within ε after time log(C/ε)/λ, so memory beyond that is impossible. Formalize the linear-stability core in Lean. Step 2 (prediction): for mass-action models, Chemical Reaction Network Theory (deficiency zero and deficiency one theorems) certifies that some networks cannot be multistable for any rates. Classify all 35 models and the random ensemble by CRNT before simulation; predict that CRNT-certified monostable networks show long-window memory only if they have slow eigenvalues (computed). Compare with approach 1's observed memory calls.
steps: State and prove the exponential-relaxation lemma for monostable systems in Lean (linear case; nonlinear case by citation of standard Lyapunov results with stated hypotheses).
Run CRNT analysis (deficiency computation) on mass-action-convertible models; compute slowest eigenvalues at steady state.
Pre-register predicted memory or no-memory per model from (multistability possible, slowest timescale).
Compare predictions with observed memory calls; report sensitivity and specificity.
approaches.decisive_result: A proved necessary condition for persistent memory, and the accuracy with which the CRNT plus slowest-timescale classification predicts observed memory across biological and random networks. High accuracy (≥ 85%) shows memory is explained by generic dynamical features, whatever the biological enrichment.
approaches.failure_signature: Many networks show memory the classification rules out, which would mean the protocol's memory criterion picks up transient effects within the test window, a finding about the protocol itself; or most models use non-mass-action kinetics outside CRNT's scope.

approaches.title: Lean: a finite complete-class theorem showing exactly when free-energy accounts are empty
approaches.method: Make the unfalsifiability charge precise, which is a result in itself. Setting: finite hidden-state space S, finite observations O, finite actions A, and a policy π: Oⁿ → A over a finite horizon. Theorem 1 (finite complete class): for every deterministic policy π there exist a generative model (prior over S, likelihood, and preference prior over outcomes) under which π minimizes expected free energy; the construction places preference mass on the outcomes π produces. So without constraints on the generative model, the claim 'morphogenesis minimizes free energy' excludes no behaviour. Theorem 2 (restoring content): if the likelihood and preference prior are fixed in advance (for example the target morphology and the cell-signalling likelihood from Friston et al. 2015's model), the set of free-energy-optimal policies is a proper subset, and there exist observable trajectories outside it, with an explicit separating example. This gives a formal criterion: an active-inference morphogenesis claim is testable iff it fixes the components named in Theorem 2.
steps: Define finite POMDP-style generative models and expected free energy over Finset types in Lean.
Prove Theorem 1 by explicit construction of the preference prior.
Prove Theorem 2 with a small explicit fixed model (for example 3 states, 2 actions) and a trajectory not optimal under it.
Write a short note mapping critics' and proponents' statements to Theorems 1 and 2.
approaches.decisive_result: Lean-checked Theorems 1 and 2. Together they state precisely that the framework is empty with a free generative model and testable with a fixed one, which turns the falsifiability debate into a checkable criterion that approaches 2 and 3 then meet.
approaches.failure_signature: Expected free energy has several non-equivalent definitions in the literature, and the theorems hold for one but not others; the result then must be stated per definition, which weakens its reach.

approaches.title: Fix Friston et al.'s generative model and derive a graded-excision prediction
approaches.method: Take the published generative model (Friston et al. 2015: cells with a shared model of target positions and signal expression) without modification and derive a quantitative prediction for an experiment that already exists. Simulate excision of fractions f ∈ {0.1, …, 0.9} of the ensemble and measure (a) time to reach the target configuration and (b) the probability of incorrect pattern (a residual error above threshold). The model predicts specific functional forms, for example recovery time increasing with f up to a critical fraction f_c beyond which the pattern fails. Freeze these predictions, functional forms and f_c with intervals over the model's stated parameter ranges, before collecting data. Then compare with published planarian regeneration data on fragment size versus regeneration success and time, and Xenopus or axolotl data where graded removals exist. Pre-registered: refuted if the observed success-versus-fragment-size curve is outside the predicted envelope at ≥ 2 fragment sizes.
steps: Reimplement the Friston et al. 2015 simulation from the published equations; reproduce its figures.
Run graded excisions over the model's parameter ranges; freeze predicted curves with envelopes.
Compile published fragment-size and regeneration-outcome data with a pre-registered inclusion rule.
Compare; report verdict and which model parameters, if any, the data constrain.
approaches.decisive_result: A pre-registered comparison of the fixed-model prediction (recovery time and failure probability versus fraction removed, with envelope) against published regeneration data. Observations outside the envelope refute this active-inference model of pattern regulation; observations inside it are a first non-trivial success.
approaches.failure_signature: The envelope over plausible parameters is so wide that it contains every monotone curve, so the fixed model still makes no risky prediction. This would confirm Theorem 1's warning in practice even with the model fixed.

approaches.title: Craniofacial remodelling: error-proportional correction vs hardwired movement
approaches.method: Xenopus 'Picasso' tadpoles, with organs experimentally displaced, remodel toward normal craniofacial geometry (Vandenberg et al. 2012; Pinet et al. 2019). A fixed-target active-inference model with Gaussian precision predicts that each organ's correction velocity is proportional to its displacement from the target, giving exponential relaxation and a rate independent of the direction of displacement. A hardwired-movement alternative (organs migrate a fixed program regardless of start) predicts velocity independent of displacement. Using organ positions reported or measurable in these papers' figures at multiple stages, estimate for each organ the regression of displacement change on initial displacement. Pre-registered: the active-inference model is supported if the slope is negative with exponential-fit R² ≥ 0.6, and refuted if velocity is independent of displacement (slope CI including 0) or if organs overshoot the target systematically, which a fixed-precision gradient flow cannot produce.
steps: Pre-register both models' predictions and the statistics.
Extract organ positions over developmental stages from the published figures and supplementary data, with landmark definitions.
Fit the displacement-dependent and displacement-independent models; compare by AICc.
Check for overshoot; report verdicts per organ.
approaches.decisive_result: Whether correction velocity scales with displacement (supporting fixed-target error correction) or not (supporting hardwired programs), per organ, with model-comparison weights. This is a risky prediction the fixed model can fail.
approaches.failure_signature: Published figures give too few time points or individuals per stage (fewer than 3 stages or 10 tadpoles), making slopes unidentifiable; or any proportional-correction result is shared by non-inferential gradient models, so it supports a class of models rather than active inference specifically (this must be stated in the interpretation).

approaches.title: Computer-assisted proof that Weaire–Phelan is a strict local minimum among periodic foams
approaches.method: Prove local optimality of the Weaire–Phelan (WP) partition within its periodic class, the result the problem asks for. Setting: partitions of the 3-torus ℝ³/Λ (the WP cubic cell, 8 cells) into cells of equal volume. WP's faces are constant-mean-curvature surfaces meeting at Plateau angles. Plan: (a) compute the WP equilibrium with Surface Evolver at high refinement with an a-posteriori error bound; (b) compute the second variation (the Jacobi operator on faces with the Plateau-border coupling conditions and volume constraints) discretized by finite elements; (c) certify, with interval arithmetic in Arb, a lower bound λ_min > 0 on the constrained Hessian's smallest non-trivial eigenvalue, modulo translations, using a residual-based enclosure (Kato–Temple or Lehmann–Goerisch bounds) that converts discrete eigenvalue estimates into rigorous bounds for the continuous operator. A positive bound proves WP is a strict local minimum against all smooth volume-preserving perturbations periodic on Λ. The same pipeline applied to Kelvin's foam reproduces known stability as a validation.
steps: Compute WP and Kelvin equilibria in Surface Evolver; validate surface areas against published values (Kelvin 5.306, WP 5.288 in units of V^(2/3) for total cell surface).
Discretize the constrained second variation; compute the lowest eigenvalues numerically.
Derive rigorous eigenvalue lower bounds with Lehmann–Goerisch and Arb interval arithmetic.
Validate on Kelvin; publish the certificate and code.
approaches.decisive_result: A certified bound λ_min > 0 for WP's constrained second variation on its periodic cell, proving strict local optimality among equal-volume partitions with that period, the first rigorous optimality-type statement for WP.
approaches.failure_signature: The discrete-to-continuous error bound for curved faces with Plateau-border junctions cannot be made rigorous with available eigenvalue-enclosure methods, or the certified margin is negative within error, leaving the result unproved.

approaches.title: Lean-checked lower bounds on equal-volume partition area
approaches.method: Prove a rigorous lower bound in Lean for surface area per cell of any partition of a 3-torus into N equal-volume cells, and state its distance from WP. Bound 1 (isoperimetric half-sphere): each cell has surface ≥ (36π)^{1/3} V^{2/3}, every interior face is shared by two cells, so partition area per cell ≥ ½(36π)^{1/3}V^{2/3} ≈ 2.418, against WP's ≈ 2.644 (half of 5.288), a gap of about 9%. This requires the 3D isoperimetric inequality, which as far as we know is not in Mathlib. Formalize it via the Brunn–Minkowski inequality for compact sets (Mathlib's measure theory supports a Prékopa–Leindler route) and the Minkowski-content definition of surface area, or state it as an explicit hypothesis in a first version. Bound 2: tighten using Kusner's face-count argument, that cells in a minimal foam have a bounded average number of faces, combined with a lower bound on the area of a polyhedral-like cell with k faces of constant curvature, giving a bound above 2.418.
steps: Survey Mathlib for Brunn–Minkowski or Prékopa–Leindler; formalize the missing piece or state the isoperimetric inequality as a hypothesis in version 1.
Prove Bound 1 for partitions of the 3-torus (shared-face accounting as a finite-sum lemma).
Formalize the face-count argument and the per-cell bound for Bound 2, if Bound 1 completes.
Report the numerical gap to WP and Kelvin.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean theorem bounding area per cell of any equal-volume 3-torus partition from below, unconditional if the isoperimetric inequality is formalized, otherwise conditional on it as a named hypothesis, with the gap to WP stated. Bound 2 above 2.418 would be new.
approaches.failure_signature: The isoperimetric inequality proves too large to formalize in a month, leaving only the conditional version, which is correct but adds little beyond the statement on paper.

references.note: Hales 2001, The honeycomb conjecture (2D analogue)

approaches.title: Scutoid frequency vs curvature in segmented 3D epithelia against minimal energy
approaches.method: Biological part. For each 3D epithelial dataset (Gómez-Gálvez et al. 2018 salivary glands and egg chambers; PlantSeg Arabidopsis ovule and lateral-root volumes as a curved plant epithelium; other open segmented volumes on IDR and EMPIAR), compute per-cell apico-basal neighbour exchanges (scutoid indicator) and the local radial expansion ratio s = R_basal/R_apical from fitted tissue surfaces. Prediction: run a 3D Voronoi tube model (Gómez-Gálvez 2018) and a Surface Evolver relaxed-foam model on a tube or ellipsoid with the measured s, cell number and cell-size dispersion, giving the predicted scutoid fraction p̂(s) with simulation intervals. Pre-registered tolerance: supports energy minimization if observed scutoid fractions fall within the 95% simulation band at ≥ 80% of curvature bins pooled across datasets; refutes if observed fractions are outside the band in the same direction in ≥ 50% of bins. Also test the Gómez-Gálvez et al. 2022 biophysical principle linking connectivity to s.
steps: Pre-register datasets' admission criteria (3D cell segmentation with apical and basal surfaces), binning of s and the tolerance.
Download and checksum datasets; compute scutoid indicators and s per cell.
Run the Voronoi and relaxed-foam simulations at measured parameters; build p̂(s) bands.
Compare and report the verdict per dataset and pooled.
approaches.decisive_result: Observed versus predicted scutoid fraction across curvature bins in at least three independent tissue types, with a pre-registered verdict on whether cells adopt minimal-energy packings for their curvature.
approaches.failure_signature: Segmentation errors in apical or basal surfaces create spurious neighbour exchanges at rates comparable to predicted scutoid fractions (estimate the error rate on manually checked cells); then the test is measurement-limited.

approaches.title: Pre-registered classifier from ZFIN labels with paralog, NMD and network features
approaches.method: Labels: from ZFIN downloads, genes with at least one morpholino phenotype and at least one phenotyped mutant allele. A gene is 'discrepant' if the mutant lacks the morphant's phenotype in the same anatomical system and stage window, and 'concordant' otherwise; this rule is fixed in advance and applied by script. Features, fixed in advance: (a) paralog structure (number of zebrafish paralogs including ohnologs from Ensembl Compara, maximum protein identity, and whether the closest paralog is co-expressed in the same tissue per ZFIN expression); (b) NMD susceptibility of the mutant allele (premature termination codon more than 50 nt upstream of the last exon junction, from allele annotation); (c) network features from INDRA CoGEx on human orthologs (degree, number of upstream regulators, membership in complexes); (d) gene length and expression level. Models: L1-regularized logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees, nested cross-validation, with a gene-family-grouped split so paralogs never span train and test. Pre-registered: success if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.70 against a feature-free baseline of 0.5 (permutation p < 0.01). Output: a ranked list of untested genes by predicted discrepancy probability.
steps: Write result.json with label rule, features, model, split and threshold before computing labels.
Download ZFIN phenotype, morpholino and allele files; Ensembl paralog tables; query CoGEx; record versions and checksums.
Construct labels and features; run nested grouped cross-validation.
Report AUROC with CI, feature importances and the ranked prediction list for genes lacking mutant data.
approaches.decisive_result: Held-out AUROC with 95% CI under gene-family-grouped cross-validation against the 0.5 baseline, plus a published ranked list of predictions for genes whose mutants are not yet phenotyped, so future ZFIN records check the prediction.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than about 150 genes have both morphant and mutant phenotypes comparable in system and stage, or AUROC CI includes 0.5: refutes predictability with present features.

approaches.title: Two-feature transcriptional-adaptation rule tested as a single hypothesis
approaches.method: Instead of a flexible classifier, test the mechanism's own prediction as one pre-registered hypothesis with no tuning. From El-Brolosy et al. 2019 and Ma et al. 2019, transcriptional adaptation requires mutant mRNA decay (an NMD-triggering PTC allele) and upregulates genes sharing sequence similarity with the mutated gene. Rule: predict 'discrepant' iff (i) the phenotyped mutant allele is PTC-bearing and NMD-sensitive and (ii) a paralog with ≥ 50% nucleotide identity over the region of similarity exists. Predict 'concordant' otherwise, including promoter-less or whole-gene deletion alleles, which the mechanism predicts do not compensate. Compute the 2 × 2 contingency table against ZFIN-derived labels (same rule as approach 1), Fisher's exact test, and the odds ratio. Pre-registered: supports if OR ≥ 3 with a 95% CI lower bound > 1.5. A natural experiment within the data: genes with both a PTC allele and a promoter-less allele phenotyped, where the mechanism predicts discordance only for the PTC allele.
steps: Pre-register the two-feature rule, identity threshold and statistics.
Annotate allele classes from ZFIN (PTC position relative to last exon junction; deletion type).
Compute paralog identities (Ensembl Compara plus nucleotide alignment of the similarity region).
Run Fisher's test; analyse the within-gene PTC versus promoter-less contrast separately.
approaches.decisive_result: Odds ratio for discrepancy given the two-feature mechanistic signature, and within-gene allele contrasts. A strong association, especially in within-gene contrasts, would turn transcriptional adaptation into a quantitative predictor; OR ≈ 1 would show it does not explain most discrepancies.
approaches.failure_signature: Too few genes have promoter-less or whole-gene-deletion alleles phenotyped (fewer than 15) for the within-gene contrast; and allele PTC annotation is missing for many ZFIN alleles.

approaches.title: Confound audit: do morpholino properties, not gene properties, predict it?
approaches.method: A rival explanation of mutant–morphant discrepancy is morpholino artefact: off-target binding and p53-mediated toxicity give phenotypes the true loss of function would not. If so, discrepancy should be predicted by properties of the morpholino, not the gene. For each morpholino in ZFIN with a target and phenotype, compute: (a) the number of off-target sites in the zebrafish transcriptome with ≤ 2 mismatches (translation-start and splice-site windows, by alignment against Ensembl transcripts); (b) whether reported phenotypes include the nonspecific toxicity signature (necrosis, pericardial oedema, small head and eyes) in the same annotations; (c) morpholino type (translation-blocking or splice-blocking) and whether rescue or p53 co-knockdown is annotated. Fit a logistic model of discrepancy on morpholino features alone, gene features alone (approach 1's), and both, with nested grouped cross-validation. Pre-registered: the artefact explanation dominates if morpholino features alone reach AUROC within 0.03 of the combined model and gene features add < 0.03.
steps: Pre-register the toxicity signature terms, off-target search parameters and comparison thresholds.
Extract morpholino sequences and targets from ZFIN; run the off-target alignment.
Fit morpholino-only, gene-only and combined models with the same splits as approach 1.
Report AUROCs and the incremental contribution of each feature group.
approaches.decisive_result: The relative predictive contribution of morpholino properties versus gene properties to mutant–morphant discrepancy. Dominance of morpholino features attributes most discrepancies to artefact; dominance of gene features supports compensation, the Frontier problem's attribution question.
approaches.failure_signature: Morpholino and gene features are confounded (genes with paralogs are also targeted by morpholinos with more off-target sites), so the incremental AUROCs cannot be separated; report the overlap instead of a verdict.
